faq.q: How many calories in Murtabak?
faq.a: A standard piece of murtabak daging (beef) at a mamak stall is around 520 calories for roughly 220g. Murtabak ayam is lighter at about 460 calories, while murtabak kambing comes in higher at around 560 calories. The murtabak kosong (egg and onion only, no meat) is the lightest at about 380 calories.

faq.q: Is murtabak good for weight loss?
faq.a: It's not a diet food, bro. At 460 to 560 calories a piece, it's a full meal on its own. That said, if you budget it into your daily calories and pair it with plain water instead of teh tarik, it fits. The beef or chicken filling gives you 25g of protein which actually keeps you full. The problem is ordering it as a snack on top of a meal, not as the meal itself.

faq.q: What's the difference in calories between murtabak ayam and murtabak daging?
faq.a: About 60 calories. Murtabak ayam is around 460 calories and murtabak daging is around 520. The gap comes from the fat content of the filling. Minced chicken is leaner than minced beef. If you're eating murtabak regularly and want to trim the numbers, switching to ayam is the easiest swap.

foods.name: Thosai (Tosai)
foods.metaDescription: Plain thosai is 170 calories per piece, making it one of the smarter mamak picks. Here's what changes that number fast.
foods.summary: A fermented rice and lentil crepe cooked on a hot tawa, thosai is one of the few mamak orders that won't immediately wreck your day.
foods.answer: Plain thosai is 170 calories for one piece (about 85g), making it one of the lighter options you can order at a mamak. The batter itself is fairly low calorie at around 125 calories, and the thin spread of cooking oil on the tawa adds another 45. Where it gets interesting is the variants: paper thosai creeps up to 200 kcal, thosai telur hits 280, and masala thosai with that potato filling lands at 320. On its own, plain thosai is genuinely not bad for the calories.
realTalk: Plain thosai at 170 calories is honestly decent for a mamak. The batter is fermented rice and urad dal, so there's a bit of protein in there (about 5g), and the carbs come in at 30g. The fat is low because a plain thosai only gets a thin wipe of oil on the tawa, around 5g of oil adding 45 calories. Compare that to roti canai which is slathered in ghee, and thosai starts looking pretty smart. Fair warning though: these are ballpark estimates. Hard nutritional data for mamak dishes is thin, and every stall's batter thickness and oil use varies, so treat 170 as a reasonable middle number, not a lab result.

The number that changes everything is what you do with it. Order masala thosai and you're at 320 calories because that spiced potato filling adds 120 to 150 kcal on its own. Thosai telur adds one egg (roughly 70-80 kcal) and puts you at 280. Then there's the sambar and coconut chutney on the side. Sambar is actually fine, maybe 30-40 kcal for a small bowl. Coconut chutney is where people get caught, it can add another 60-80 kcal depending on how oily the stall makes it. If you're watching your numbers, plain thosai with sambar is a solid 200-calorie breakfast. Add a thosai telur and you're still at a reasonable 320 with actual protein to show for it.
lighter: Order plain (kosong) instead of masala. That alone saves you 150 calories from skipping the potato filling.
Go with sambar over coconut chutney. Sambar is mostly lentil broth and vegetables. Coconut chutney has a lot more fat and calories.
Thosai telur is actually a good trade if you're hungry. You add one egg for 70-80 kcal but you get proper protein which keeps you full longer.
Ask the uncle to go easy on the oil. Most will do it if you ask. It won't crisp up the same but you're saving maybe 20-30 kcal.
Two plain thosai is about 340 calories total and genuinely filling. That beats one masala thosai at 320 because you're getting more volume and less potato carbs.

faq.q: Is thosai good for weight loss?
faq.a: Plain thosai is one of the lighter mamak options at 170 calories a piece. It's not a protein powerhouse (only 5g protein), but paired with sambar and maybe a thosai telur, it's a reasonable low-calorie breakfast that won't leave you starving by 10am.

faq.q: Which is healthier, thosai or roti canai?
faq.a: Plain thosai wins easily. One plain thosai is about 170 calories with 4g fat. One roti canai plain is around 300 calories with significantly more fat from the ghee and dough folding. If you're at the mamak and watching calories, thosai is the smarter pick.

foods.name: Vadai
foods.metaDescription: One vadai has 195 calories. Here's the honest breakdown of what's driving those numbers and how many you can actually eat before it wrecks your deficit.
foods.summary: A crispy deep-fried lentil fritter from the mamak, made with spiced dhal batter and available plain or with a prawn on top.
foods.answer: One piece of vadai (about 60g) has 195 calories. That is not a lot for something this satisfying, but the catch is nobody eats just one. The calories come mostly from the dhal batter at 115 kcal and the oil absorbed during deep frying at 70 kcal. The spices and onion are basically free. So yes, 195 per piece is the honest number for a standard mamak medu vadai.
realTalk: Vadai gets a bit of a free pass because it sounds healthy, lentils lah, whole spices, no sugar. And honestly 195 kcal per piece is not outrageous. But 70 of those calories are pure absorbed frying oil. That is more than a third of the entire piece just from oil. The lentil batter does bring some protein and a bit of fibre, so it is not completely empty, but calling this a light snack would be wishful thinking. One piece is fine. The problem is the mamak charges like RM1.50 per piece and they come out hot and crispy and before you know it you have eaten four of them.

The real variable here is how many pieces you eat and what you dip it in. Four dhal vadai straight up is 780 kcal. Add two generous scoops of coconut chutney at roughly 60 kcal each and you are sitting at 900 kcal for what felt like a light snack. Prawn vadai bumps each piece to 215 kcal because of the prawn on top but also adds a bit more protein, so if you are eating two pieces anyway the prawn version is not a bad trade. The other thing that changes the maths is whether you are eating this as a starter before a full nasi kandar plate or as a standalone. Standalone, two pieces at 390 kcal is a decent snack. As a starter before a big meal, you probably did not need them.
lighter: Stop at one or two pieces. The per-piece number is reasonable but vadai is dangerously easy to eat four or five without thinking.
Skip the coconut chutney if you are watching calories. A generous scoop can add 50 to 80 kcal on top of the vadai itself.
Choose dhal vadai over prawn vadai if you want to save about 20 kcal per piece. Small difference but it adds up.
Eat it as part of a meal rather than a standalone snack. Paired with a teh tarik kosong and some protein, it fills you up properly instead of just teasing your stomach.
At home, you can air fry lentil patties and cut the oil absorption significantly. Not quite the same crunch, but the calories drop by 40 to 50 kcal per piece.

faq.q: How many calories in Vadai?
faq.a: One piece of vadai weighs about 60g and has 195 calories. That covers 5g protein, 14g carbs, and 13g fat. Prawn vadai runs slightly higher at around 215 kcal because of the prawn on top.

faq.q: Is vadai healthy or just empty calories?
faq.a: It is not empty calories exactly. You are getting lentil protein and some fibre from the dhal batter. The problem is the deep frying soaks up around 8g of oil per piece, which adds 70 kcal before you even count the batter. One or two pieces alongside a proper meal is fine. Eating five pieces as a snack is where the numbers get away from you.

faq.q: How does vadai compare to roti canai for calories?
faq.a: Roti canai plain is around 300 kcal for a full piece while vadai is 195 kcal per piece. But roti canai is bigger and more filling, so the comparison is not quite fair. Per gram, they are actually pretty similar because both are cooked in a lot of oil or fat. If you are just grabbing something quick at the mamak, one vadai is fewer calories than one roti canai.

foods.name: Idli
foods.serving: 2 pieces with sambar and coconut chutney
foods.metaDescription: Idli with sambar and coconut chutney is 275 calories per standard mamak plate. One of the lightest things you can order. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Steamed fermented rice cakes served with lentil sambar and coconut chutney, and one of the few mamak orders that won't wreck your calorie budget.
foods.answer: A standard mamak idli plate (2 pieces with sambar and coconut chutney) comes in at 275 calories for about 220g of food. The steamed rice cakes themselves are only 130 calories; the sambar adds another 80 and the coconut chutney brings 65. So the sides are doing nearly half the calorie work here. For a mamak order, 275 calories is genuinely one of the lightest things you can pick off the menu.
realTalk: 275 calories for a full mamak plate is genuinely impressive. The idli cakes themselves are only 130 calories for two pieces, steamed with zero oil, which is basically unheard of at a mamak. The sambar chips in 80 calories and brings actual protein from the lentils, so it's not just empty carbs. The coconut chutney is where most people don't think twice, but those 30g add 65 calories mostly from coconut fat. It's still not a lot. If you're the kind of person who was 110kg and eating roti canai with three teh tariks for breakfast, switching to idli is honestly a cheat code.

What actually changes the maths is the oil and the portion size. Plain idli with just sambar drops you to 210 calories, so skipping the coconut chutney saves 65 without losing much enjoyment. The dangerous version is masala idli, where the cakes get tossed in spiced oil with vegetables and suddenly you're at 320 calories. Still not terrible by mamak standards, but you've added almost 50 calories from oil you probably didn't think about. Sambar is the better side to double up on if you're still hungry, it's mostly lentils and vegetables and won't move the needle much. Two orders of plain idli with sambar comes to 420 calories, which for most people is a perfectly filling breakfast.
lighter: Order idli with sambar only and skip the coconut chutney to cut 65 calories and drop to 210 total.
Avoid masala idli. The spiced oil toss adds roughly 45 calories compared to the standard plate.
If you want more volume, ask for extra sambar instead of extra chutney. Sambar is mostly lentils and vegetables, so the calorie cost per spoon is much lower.
Pair with plain water or a small kopi-o kosong instead of teh tarik, or you've doubled the calorie count of the whole meal.
Two orders of plain idli with sambar is still only around 420 calories and much more filling than one roti canai.

faq.q: Is idli good for weight loss?
faq.a: Yes, it's one of the best mamak options if you're watching calories. The cakes are steamed with no oil, and the sambar gives you some protein from lentils. Just watch the coconut chutney and avoid masala idli if you want to keep things light.

faq.q: How does idli compare to roti canai for calories?
faq.a: Idli wins easily. A standard roti canai with dhal is around 360 to 400 calories, and that's before you add curry. Idli with sambar and chutney is 275 calories, and you get more volume for the price.

foods.name: Sup Kambing
foods.metaDescription: Sup Kambing with bread clocks around 520 calories. Here's what drives the number and how to keep it lower without skipping the good stuff.
foods.summary: A rich, warming spiced mutton soup served with French bread, the kind you find at mamak stalls at midnight when you need something real.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of Sup Kambing with 2 slices of French bread comes to around 520 calories. That breaks down as roughly 220 kcal from the bone-in mutton, 85 kcal from the spiced broth, 185 kcal from the bread, and 30 kcal from the veg and garnish. If you skip the bread and just have the soup, you're looking at about 340 calories instead, which is actually a pretty decent protein hit for the calories.
realTalk: 520 calories for a full bowl with bread is honestly not bad for how satisfying this soup is. The mutton itself is doing the heavy lifting on protein, about 32g per bowl, which is solid. The fat comes mostly from two places: the mutton itself (bone-in cuts like ribs and shank have good marbling) and the rendered fat sitting in the broth. That broth is around 85 kcal for 300ml, which sounds innocent until you realize some stalls are ladling in way more oil than others. Fair warning: these are ballpark estimates. Hard nutrition data for Sup Kambing is thin, so treat this as a reasonable middle-ground figure rather than a lab result.

The biggest variable in the maths is what you eat it with. Skip the 2 slices of French bread (70g, 185 kcal) and your bowl drops from 520 to around 340 calories, which is genuinely low for how full you feel. Swap to roti canai instead and you're pushing 620 kcal. The other lever is the broth. Some stalls serve it cleaner, some are swimming in ghee. If you're watching intake, ask for less oil in the soup, it actually works at the good stalls. The mutton portion also varies a lot. The 200g bone-in weight here gives you roughly 110g of edible meat, so if your stall is more generous, add roughly 20 kcal per extra 10g of meat.
lighter: Order soup only, no bread. You cut 185 kcal straight away and the soup is still filling on its own.
Ask the uncle to go easy on the oil when ladling. A less greasy broth can save you 30 to 50 kcal without losing flavour.
Avoid dunking the bread in the broth repeatedly. Bread soaks up oil fast and those calories add up quick.
If you want something to dip, ask if they have plain buns or less oily bread options. The French bread is pretty calorie-dense for its size.
Eat the meat, leave some of the fattier broth at the bottom of the bowl. The spice flavour is in the early sips anyway.

faq.a: A standard bowl of Sup Kambing with 2 slices of French bread is around 520 calories. If you have just the soup and mutton without any bread, it drops to about 340 calories.

faq.q: Is Sup Kambing good for weight loss?
faq.a: The soup itself is actually decent for dieting. 340 calories with around 26-27g of protein is a solid deal. The bread is where the extra calories pile in. Skip or reduce the bread and it becomes one of the more filling low-calorie options at the mamak.

faq.q: Why is Sup Kambing high in fat?
faq.a: Mutton, especially bone-in cuts like ribs and shank, naturally carries more fat than chicken. On top of that, the broth is cooked with rendered fat and sometimes ghee or oil added at the stall. The fat count per bowl is around 28g, most of it coming from the meat and the oily broth.

foods.name: Sup Tulang
foods.metaDescription: Sup Tulang is around 350 calories per bowl (clear broth). Sup tulang merah jumps to 480 cal. Here's what's actually driving the numbers.
foods.summary: Slow-cooked mutton or beef leg bones in a deeply spiced broth, with rich marrow that you suck straight out of the bone.
foods.answer: A bowl of Sup Tulang comes in at around 350 calories for a standard serving of 2 to 3 bones with broth (about 400g total). Most of that comes from the bone marrow alone, which clocks in at roughly 170 calories from just 22g of the stuff. The meat on the bone adds another 140 calories, and the spiced broth keeps things relatively lean at 50 calories. For a full bone soup with that much richness and flavour, 350 calories is honestly pretty reasonable.
realTalk: Sup tulang sits at around 350 calories per bowl for the clear version, and honestly that's not bad at all for how satisfying it is. You're getting 26g of protein, which is solid, but the fat is also 26g and that's mostly coming from the bone marrow. That 22g of marrow packs 170 calories on its own, bro. It's basically concentrated fat in a hollow bone, which is exactly why it tastes so good when you suck it out. The meat off the bone adds another 140 cal, the broth is a light 50 cal, and the tendon and cartilage contribute 30 cal. Worth noting: these are ballpark estimates because detailed nutritional data for sup tulang specifically is quite thin, so treat the 350 cal figure as a reasonable guide rather than a precise count.

The version that actually messes with your tracking is sup tulang merah, which runs around 480 calories per bowl. That extra 130 calories comes from the red rempah sauce made with ghee, tomato puree, chilli paste, and sugar. Same bones, completely different calorie story. So if you're at a gerai and they ask which one you want, the clear broth saves you a meaningful chunk. Practical tips: skip soaking your bread in the broth (that soaked-in roti adds calories fast), ask for less sauce on the merah version, and don't go back for a second helping of the marrow bones if you're watching intake. The soup itself is actually your friend here. It fills you up, it's warm, and the protein from the meat is real.
lighter: Order the clear broth version (sup tulang) instead of merah to save around 130 calories per bowl.
Skip dipping bread or roti into the broth. It tastes great but adds calories quickly and there's no fixed amount people stop at.
Eat the meat off the bone but go easy on how much marrow you suck out. Each bone has roughly 7 to 8g of marrow, and it adds up fast.
Ask the stall to go light on the ghee or oil if you're getting the merah version. Some places are more generous than others.
Pair it with plain rice rather than nasi goreng or roti on the side. The soup is already filling enough on its own.

faq.q: Is Sup Tulang good for weight loss?
faq.a: It's not bad, honestly. 350 calories for a bowl that's warm, filling, and has 26g of protein is a reasonable deal. The issue is the bone marrow, which is pure fat. If you're in a deficit, clear broth sup tulang can fit into your day. Avoid the merah version if you're being strict.

faq.q: Why does Sup Tulang Merah have so many more calories?
faq.a: The bones themselves are the same, so the protein and marrow content is identical. The extra calories come from the rempah sauce: ghee, tomato puree, chilli paste, and a bit of sugar. That sauce adds around 130 calories to the bowl compared to the clear broth version.

foods.name: Sup Ekor
foods.metaDescription: Sup Ekor has around 500 calories per bowl (no rice). Here's what's driving the number and whether oxtail soup fits into a diet.
foods.summary: Rich, slow-simmered oxtail soup with a fatty collagen broth, potato, and carrot, a bowl that delivers serious protein but does not pretend to be light.
foods.answer: A bowl of Sup Ekor comes in at around 500 calories for a standard serving (550g, no rice). That might sound reasonable until you realise most of those calories are coming from the oxtail itself and the rich, collagen-heavy broth, not from carbs. The meat alone clocks about 300 calories, and the broth adds another 120. So yes, it is a protein-forward bowl, but the fat content is real, at 28g per serving.
realTalk: Sup Ekor is honestly one of those soups that feels healthy because it is a soup, but the numbers tell a different story. At 500 calories a bowl, it is not a disaster by any means, but the 28g of fat should not surprise anyone. Oxtail is a tough, collagen-rich cut that has been simmered for hours, and all that rendered fat goes straight into the broth. The meat itself gives you a solid 38g of protein, which is actually great, but you are not getting lean chicken breast here. Fair disclaimer: the exact numbers for this dish are harder to pin down than your average hawker food. Sup Ekor varies a lot by stall and kitchen, so treat this 500 calorie figure as a reasonable ballpark estimate, not a precise measurement.

What really changes the maths here is portion size and how much broth you drink. A restaurant or hotel version can push up to 650 calories because they serve bigger oxtail pieces and often reduce the broth further, concentrating the fat. The fried shallot garnish adds another 45 calories and it is easy to ignore because it looks like a tiny sprinkle. Then there is rice. If you add a standard 200g plate of white rice, you go from 500 to 760 calories total. That is a heavy meal lah. The soup by itself with the oxtail and vegetables is actually a high-protein, reasonable option if you eat it as is and leave some of the broth behind.
lighter: Skip the rice or have half a plate instead of a full one. That alone saves you 130 to 260 calories.
Do not drink all the broth. The bottom of the bowl is where the rendered fat pools. Leave 50 to 100ml behind and you cut maybe 40 to 60 calories without losing much of the experience.
Ask for less fried shallot garnish or skip it. It is only 45 calories but they fry it in oil, so it adds up fast if the stall is generous.
Order Sup Ayam instead if you want the soup experience with lower fat. Chicken soup runs around 150 to 200 calories lighter than oxtail.
Eat this for lunch rather than dinner so you have the rest of the day to move around. A 500-calorie soup lunch is actually quite manageable if you are tracking.

faq.q: How many calories in Sup Ekor?
faq.a: A standard bowl of Sup Ekor (550g, no rice) has around 500 calories. Add white rice and you are looking at roughly 760 calories for the full meal.

faq.q: Is Sup Ekor good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can work, honestly. 38g of protein per bowl is solid, and you are getting a proper filling meal. The catch is the fat content, 28g per bowl, mostly from the oxtail and the broth. If you skip the rice and do not drink the entire broth, it fits reasonably well into a calorie deficit.

faq.q: Why is oxtail soup so high in calories?
faq.a: Oxtail is a fatty cut of beef. Unlike chicken breast, you cannot really separate the fat out before eating it because it is marbled into the meat and dissolved into the broth during the long simmer. That broth alone adds about 120 calories just from the rendered fat and collagen.

foods.name: Sup Ayam
foods.metaDescription: Sup Ayam comes in at around 250 calories per bowl. One of the lighter hawker soups you can order. Here's what drives the numbers.
foods.summary: Clear spiced chicken soup with bone-in pieces, potato, carrot, and a fragrant broth, one of the lighter soups you will find at a Malaysian hawker stall.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of Sup Ayam comes in at around 250 calories for a 430g bowl. That includes the chicken pieces, the clear spiced broth, potato, carrot, and a sprinkle of fried shallots on top. For a hawker soup, that is genuinely on the lighter side. Most of the calories come from the chicken, not the broth, which is good news if you are watching your intake.
realTalk: Sup Ayam is genuinely one of the better things you can order at a hawker stall when you are trying to watch your calories without suffering. At roughly 250 calories for a full bowl, it gives you 25g of protein and actually fills you up because of the volume, 430g of food for a quarter of your daily calories is a solid deal. The bulk of the calories come from the chicken itself, which clocks in at 140 calories, while the broth is basically free at 30 calories for 300ml. To be fair, these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid nutrition data for local hawker Sup Ayam is thin, and every stall makes their broth differently, so treat the 250 figure as a reasonable middle ground, not a lab result.

What actually changes the maths is what you do around the soup. Add a plate of white rice on the side and you jump from 250 to about 450 calories, that is 200 calories of rice doing the damage, not the soup. The fried shallots on top add around 20 calories for just 5g, which sounds small but that is because they are basically little oil bombs, so if the stall is heavy-handed with the garnish, it adds up. If you are watching fat, peel the chicken skin off before eating, the meat itself is lean. And if you are trying to hit a protein target, this bowl at 25g of protein per serving is doing real work for you, bro.
lighter: Skip or peel off the chicken skin before eating. It does not seem like much but the skin carries a good chunk of the fat.
Ask for less potato if you want to cut carbs. The potato chunks add about 50 calories and are the main carb source in the bowl.
Eat it without rice on the side. The moment you add a plate of white rice, you are looking at 450 calories instead of 250.
Order the sayur-heavy version if the stall has it. Sup ayam sayur comes in around 120 calories because it swaps most of the chicken for vegetables.
Do not drink every drop of the broth if you are watching sodium. The sodium is not a calorie issue, but it will make you retain water and feel bloated.

faq.q: Is Sup Ayam good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, yes. It is one of the better hawker options. High protein from the chicken, low-calorie broth, and 250 calories total means you can eat a full bowl and not blow your day. Just skip adding rice, or at least account for it.

faq.q: Does Sup Ayam have a lot of fat?
faq.a: Not really. A standard bowl has around 7g of fat, mostly from the chicken skin and the small amount of fried shallots on top. If you skip the skin, you bring that number down a bit further.

foods.name: Sup Gear Box
foods.serving: 1 bowl (1 large knee bone with broth)
foods.metaDescription: Sup Gear Box has around 420 calories per bowl with marrow, or 290 kcal if you skip sucking the bone. Here's the full calorie breakdown.
foods.summary: A rich Malaysian beef knee joint soup where the real prize is the marrow you suck straight out of the bone with a straw.
foods.answer: Sup Gear Box comes in at around 420 calories for a standard bowl with one large knee joint, broth, and full marrow. Most of that comes from the beef shank meat (about 270 kcal) and the bone marrow you suck out (120 kcal), with the broth adding almost nothing. It is genuinely one of the higher-protein soups you can get at a hawker, packing 33g of protein in a single bowl.
realTalk: Honest answer: 420 kcal is a fair estimate for a standard bowl, but this is genuinely hard to pin down precisely because every stall makes it differently. Bone size varies, some joints are meatier, and the amount of marrow you actually extract changes everything. Treat these numbers as a reasonable ballpark, not lab-tested figures. The biggest driver of calories here is not the meat or the broth, it is the marrow. That 35g of marrow packs 120 kcal on its own, pure fat, and it is so easy to eat because it basically melts. The beef shank meat itself is actually great for dieting: lean, high protein, and very filling. Bro, 180g of cooked beef shank with 33g total protein in a bowl is not bad at all.

What actually changes the maths is whether you eat the marrow or not. Skip it and you are looking at 290 kcal, eat it all and you are at 420. Some stalls give you a massive joint or even two bones, and then you are easily at 750 kcal or more before you even add rice. The broth is almost a free pass at around 25 kcal for 300ml, so drink as much as you want. If you want to eat this regularly while losing weight, the move is simple: order one bone, eat all the meat and cartilage, leave the marrow or only eat half. You still get a hot, filling, protein-heavy meal for under 300 kcal. That is a win lah.
lighter: Skip sucking the marrow entirely. That one move removes 120 kcal and most of the fat from the bowl, bringing you down to around 290 kcal.
Ask for a smaller bone or a single joint only. Some stalls will serve two bones by default and that can push you to 750 kcal.
Eat it without rice or with just a small portion. The soup and meat alone are already filling because of all the collagen and protein.
Do not drink all the broth if the stall uses a lot of oil. The broth itself is low calorie but heavily oiled versions can add hidden calories.
Order it as a late lunch rather than dinner. The fat from marrow is fine in moderation but eating a 420-calorie soup late at night on top of everything else adds up fast.

It tastes rich and buttery, but it adds about 120 kcal and most of the fat in the bowl. Worth it occasionally, but if you are watching calories, just leave it.

foods.name: Tomyam
foods.metaDescription: Tomyam campur (clear broth) is about 250 calories per bowl. Here's what drives the number and which version is actually diet-friendly.
foods.summary: A sour, spicy mixed soup that is one of the more calorie-friendly things you can order at a hawker, as long as you pick the right version.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of tomyam campur (clear broth, 400g) comes in at around 250 calories. That's actually pretty decent for a full bowl of soup with real protein in it. You're getting 22g of protein from the mixed seafood and chicken, the broth itself is mostly water with aromatics, and the vegetables add almost nothing calorie-wise. The fat sits at 12g, mostly from the chili paste base and a bit of cooking oil. For a hawker dish, 250 cal is genuinely on the lighter side. The ayam version comes in lowest at around 200 cal, mostly because campur bowls tend to include fattier fish fillet cuts and vary more in how much oil goes in, which pushes the calorie count up slightly compared to a straight chicken bowl.
realTalk: Tomyam is genuinely one of the better options at a hawker stall if you are watching calories. A standard bowl of campur, clear broth, 400g, comes in around 250 calories with 22g of protein from the mixed prawns, squid, fish and chicken. The broth is mostly water, lemongrass, galangal, chili and fish sauce, so it adds very little. The calories are mostly from the protein and the chili paste base cooked with oil. That said, these numbers are ballpark estimates because hard data for Malaysian hawker food is thin. Different stalls use different amounts of oil, different ratios of paste, different amounts of protein. Treat 250 as a reasonable middle estimate, not a lab-verified figure.

What actually changes the maths here is a) how heavy-handed the cook is with cooking oil and b) whether you ordered putih or clear. The clear broth version stays under 260 calories pretty comfortably. Order tomyam putih (the creamy one with santan) and you are adding roughly 90 calories from 50ml of coconut milk, pushing the bowl to about 340 calories. That is 36% more calories from one ingredient swap, bro. The ayam version (chicken only) actually comes in lowest at around 200 cal. Chicken breast and most seafood like prawns and squid are roughly similar in leanness, but campur bowls tend to include fattier cuts like fish fillet and vary more in how much oil goes in, which pushes the calorie count up slightly. If you are eating this as a main and want to keep calories low, go clear broth, ask for extra protein, skip the rice on the side.
lighter: Order clear broth, not putih. That one swap saves you about 90 calories from the coconut milk.
Ask the stall to go light on the oil or chili paste base. Most places use a pre-mixed paste and the amount varies wildly between stalls.
Eat the tomyam on its own without rice. It is filling enough as a standalone, especially with the protein in it.
Choose chicken breast (ayam version) over campur if you want the lowest calorie option, around 200 cal versus 250.
Don't drink all the broth if you are watching sodium. The flavour is in the solids, the broth just adds salt and a bit of oil at the bottom of the bowl.

foods.name: Bubur Ayam
foods.metaDescription: Bubur Ayam has 330 calories per bowl. Here's what's actually in it, what pushes the number up, and how to eat it without blowing your day.
foods.summary: Warm rice congee with shredded chicken, fried shallots, and spring onion, a light but surprisingly filling bowl at 330 calories.
foods.answer: Bubur Ayam comes in at 330 calories per bowl (400g), making it one of the more diet-friendly options you can order at the mamak. That number is for the full standard version with shredded chicken breast, fried shallots, spring onion, and a sesame oil and soy sauce drizzle. You're getting 22g of protein and 42g of carbs, so it's genuinely filling without wrecking your calorie budget for the day.
realTalk: 330 calories for a full bowl of chicken congee is genuinely not bad lah. Think about it, you're getting a warm, filling 400g bowl with real protein from the chicken and enough carbs to feel human again. The congee base itself is only 135 calories because it's mostly water that the rice soaked up during cooking. The shredded chicken breast at 75g adds 110 calories and that's where your 22g of protein comes from. The sneaky calories are the fried shallots (40 cal) and that sesame oil drizzle (45 cal), which sounds small but together that's 85 calories for stuff that sits on top. This is a solid breakfast or sick-day meal for someone trying to lose weight.

What actually changes the maths is how heavy-handed the stall is with the oil and shallots. Some places pour on the sesame oil like it's free, easily doubling that 45 calorie estimate to 90 or more. Add a side of keropok and you're suddenly at 430 calories before you even touch your teh tarik. The big win here is swapping to plain congee with extra chicken, so 135 calories base plus 110 calories of chicken gets you to 245 calories with solid protein and none of the fried bits. If you add an egg instead of keropok, you're at around 400 calories with even more protein. Bro that's a legit high-volume, decent-protein meal for someone trying to be in a deficit.
lighter: Skip the keropok and crackers on the side, that's an easy 100 calories you don't really taste anyway.
Ask for less oil drizzle or no sesame oil. That 5g drizzle accounts for 45 calories, which is a lot for something you barely notice.
Double up on the shredded chicken instead of adding an egg if you want more protein without ballooning the calories too much.
Go easy on the fried shallots. They're delicious but 8g is already 40 calories and some stalls pile them on way more generously than that.
Eat it without soy sauce if you're also watching sodium, especially if you're retaining water and wondering why the scale won't move.

faq.q: Is Bubur Ayam good for weight loss?

faq.q: Why does congee feel so filling even though it's mostly rice?
faq.a: Rice congee is cooked with way more water than normal rice, so the volume is much higher per calorie. Add some chicken on top and you're sorted.

foods.name: Bubur Lambuk
foods.metaDescription: Bubur Lambuk has about 350 calories per bowl. Here's what's driving that number and how the mosque version compares to the restaurant one.
foods.summary: A Ramadan spiced rice porridge cooked with meat, coconut milk and aromatics, most famous from mosque free distributions every evening.
foods.answer: One bowl of Bubur Lambuk (350g) comes in at around 350 calories. That's for the standard mosque-distribution style with minced beef, dried shrimp, moderate coconut milk and the usual spices. It's not a low-calorie food but it's not a calorie bomb either, sitting somewhere in the middle compared to other Malaysian one-bowl meals.
realTalk: 350 calories for a bowl of bubur lambuk is honestly pretty reasonable for a full one-dish meal, bro. The rice base is only 150 calories because it's been cooked down into porridge with a ton of water, so you're getting a lot of volume for not that many carbs. The calories actually come mostly from the coconut milk (60 calories in just 40ml) and the cooking oil or ghee with the aromatics (55 calories worth). The meat at 65 calories is the most useful part nutritionally, giving you 18g protein which is solid for a porridge. Fair warning though: hard data on bubur lambuk is thin, so treat this as a ballpark estimate. The mosque recipe varies every year depending on who's cooking, and the quantities of santan and ghee are not exactly standardized.

What really changes the maths is how heavy-handed the cook is with the santan and ghee. The mosque version at 350 calories uses moderate coconut milk. A restaurant version with full santan and generous ghee jumps to around 430 calories, same bowl size, just creamier. On the lighter end, the vegan version with minimal coconut milk and no meat drops to about 220 calories, which is genuinely low for a filling bowl of porridge. If you're collecting your free bubur at the masjid during Ramadan and you want to keep it sensible, the portion size matters too. A smaller bowl at 250g is probably closer to 250 calories. The gravy at the bottom of the container is where most of the fat hides, so if you're watching it, go easy on ladling that last bit out.
lighter: Ask for less gravy at the bottom of the pot, that's where the coconut milk and ghee concentrate
Go for the chicken version over beef if you have a choice, saves you about 50 calories a bowl
Stick to one bowl and pair with plain vegetables rather than a second helping
Skip the crackers or keropok on the side, those add 80 to 120 calories real fast
If you're making it at home, swap half the coconut milk for low-fat evaporated milk and cut ghee to 5g instead of 10g

faq.q: How many calories in Bubur Lambuk?
faq.a: A standard 350g bowl of Bubur Lambuk has around 350 calories. That's the typical mosque-style version with minced beef, moderate coconut milk and spices. A lighter chicken version is closer to 300 calories, and a rich restaurant version with more santan can reach 430 calories.

faq.q: Is Bubur Lambuk healthy or fattening?
faq.a: It's actually one of the more balanced Ramadan foods lah. You get 18g of protein from the meat, a reasonable 40g of carbs from the porridge base, and the volume of the bowl keeps you full. The fat (12g) mostly comes from coconut milk and ghee. Compared to something like nasi lemak or murtabak, it's pretty manageable if you don't go back for a second bowl.

faq.q: Why is Bubur Lambuk so popular during Ramadan?
faq.a: Mosques all over Malaysia distribute it free every evening during Ramadan, especially Masjid Kampung Baru in KL which has been doing it for decades. It's a tradition more than anything. Nutritionally it works well too because it's easy to digest after a long fast, and the rice porridge base sits comfortably in your stomach without wrecking you before Terawih prayers.

foods.name: Yong Tau Foo (Soup)
foods.serving: 1 bowl (8 pieces, clear soup, no noodles)
foods.metaDescription: Yong Tau Foo soup (8 pieces, clear broth) is about 300 calories. Here's what changes that number and how to order it smarter.
foods.summary: Stuffed tofu, fish paste items, and vegetables in a clear anchovy broth, one of the most diet-friendly bowls at any hawker centre if you pick your pieces right.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of Yong Tau Foo soup (8 pieces, clear broth, no noodles) comes in at around 300 calories. That is a pretty solid number for a meal that actually fills you up, and it is one of the better options you will find at a hawker stall if you are watching what you eat. The clear anchovy broth itself is almost nothing calorie-wise; most of the calories come from the fish paste stuffed into the tofu, bitter gourd, and eggplant pieces.
realTalk: Bro, Yong Tau Foo soup is genuinely one of the hawker stall MVPs for anyone trying to eat less. Around 300 calories for a proper 8-piece bowl in clear broth, with 24g of protein from all that fish paste, is hard to beat. The broth itself is basically free at only 25 calories for 250g of soup. To be straight with you though, that 300 figure is a solid ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for YTF is thin and every stall stuffs their pieces differently. Some auntie might pack twice the fish paste into her bitter gourd, and suddenly your 170-calorie stuffed items column is off. Use 300 as a working number, not gospel.

What actually changes the maths is your piece selection and whether you go dry or soup. One or two fried pieces like tau pok or fried tofu skin sneaks in an extra 50-70 kcal right away. Go for the soup version and stick to tofu, bitter gourd, okra, fish balls, and eggplant and you are looking at closer to 280 calories. Swap to the dry version with sweet sauce and you are at 360 before you even add noodles. Add bee hoon or kway tiao and the bowl jumps to around 480 calories lah. The good news is you have full control at the ordering stage, which is more than you can say for most hawker dishes.
lighter: Go full clear soup, no fried pieces at all. Fried tau pok or fried tofu skin adds 50-70 kcal just from 1-2 pieces, and honestly you barely notice the difference in taste.
Skip or halve the sweet chili or hoisin dipping sauce. That sauce alone adds around 60 calories and it is mostly sugar.
Skip the noodles entirely or ask for a smaller portion. No noodles saves you 150-180 kcal.
Load up on the vegetable pieces like bitter gourd, okra, and eggplant rather than multiple fish tofu pieces. More volume, fewer calories.
Avoid the dry version served with thick sauce. The soup version keeps everything lighter and you still get a satisfying bowl.

faq.q: How many calories in Yong Tau Foo (Soup)?
faq.a: A bowl with 8 pieces in clear soup and no noodles is roughly 300 calories. Keep in mind this is a ballpark figure since the exact count depends heavily on which pieces you pick and how much fish paste is stuffed into each item.

faq.q: Is Yong Tau Foo good for weight loss?
faq.a: It is genuinely one of the better hawker options out there. High protein from all the fish paste, relatively low fat if you stick to the clear soup version, and it is filling enough that you are not hungry again in an hour. Just skip the fried pieces and go easy on the sweet sauce.

faq.q: Does adding noodles to Yong Tau Foo make a big difference?
faq.a: Yes, a fair bit. Adding bee hoon or kway tiao bumps the total up to around 480 calories, so you are looking at an extra 150-180 kcal. If you are cutting calories, go noodle-free or ask for less noodles.

foods.name: Hakka Lei Cha (Thunder Tea Rice)
foods.metaDescription: Hakka Lei Cha (Thunder Tea Rice) has 430 calories per bowl. Lots of vegetables, herb broth, but watch the peanut topping. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: A Hakka rice bowl loaded with stir-fried vegetables and poured over with a fragrant herb tea broth, one of the genuinely lighter hawker meals you can order without feeling guilty.
foods.answer: Hakka Lei Cha (Thunder Tea Rice) comes in at 430 calories per bowl (roughly 400g). That is genuinely not bad for a full rice meal. The rice itself accounts for 195 of those calories, the mixed vegetables add only 80, and the herb broth is basically free at 30. What nudges the number up is the peanut and sesame topping, which is 75 calories in just 15 grams. So yes, the "healthy" dish has its traps, but all things considered, 430 cal for a proper filling bowl is a solid deal.
realTalk: Lei Cha is probably one of the most underrated hawker options if you are watching your calories. At 430 calories for a full bowl, you are getting rice, a mountain of vegetables, tofu, anchovies, and that earthy herb broth all at once. The vegetables and broth do almost nothing to the calorie count, which is the whole point. The real calorie driver is the peanut and sesame topping, 75 calories in just 15 grams. That tiny pile of nuts costs you almost as much as 100g of cooked rice. Most people do not even think about it because it looks like a garnish, but it is basically nut butter territory in terms of calorie density.

What actually moves the number up or down is simple. The oil used when stir-frying those vegetables varies a lot between stalls. A heavy-handed wok with extra oil can easily add 50 to 80 calories across the vegetable portion. The peanut portion is the other lever: ask for less topping and you drop about 35 to 50 calories without losing any satisfaction from the meal. If you swap white rice for brown rice the calorie count stays roughly the same at 430, but you get more fibre which helps you feel full longer. And if you ask the stall to go easy on the chai por (preserved radish), you are also cutting a bit of sodium, which matters if you are retaining water.
lighter: Ask for half the peanut and sesame topping. You save roughly 35 calories and you honestly still taste it.
Request less oil on the stir-fried vegetables. Lei Cha stalls vary wildly here and it can add up to 80 extra calories silently.
Take a smaller rice portion, say 120g instead of 150g. That shaves about 32 calories and the bowl still looks huge because of the vegetables.
Skip or reduce the chai por (preserved radish). Lower sodium means less water retention, which shows up on the scale faster than you think.
Add more broth. The herb tea broth is only 30 calories per 100g, so asking for extra keeps the bowl satisfying without touching the calorie count much.

faq.a: A standard bowl of Hakka Lei Cha is 430 calories. That covers the rice, stir-fried vegetables, tofu, anchovies, peanut topping, and herb broth together.

faq.q: Is Lei Cha good for weight loss?
faq.a: Bah, it is one of the better hawker options honestly. 430 calories for a full bowl is solid. The vegetables and broth are low calorie and filling. Just go easy on the peanut topping, that is where most of the fat comes from.

faq.q: What makes Lei Cha high or low calorie?
faq.a: The peanuts and sesame seeds are the main variable, 75 calories in just 15 grams. After that, how much oil the stall uses on the stir-fried vegetables can swing the total by 50 to 80 calories. The herb broth itself is barely 30 calories per 100g.

foods.name: Steamboat
foods.serving: 1 serving per person (mixed meats, seafood, noodles, veg, clear or mild broth)
foods.metaDescription: Steamboat calories: around 750 cal for a typical Malaysian hawker serve. Mala broth version hits 1,200. Here's what actually moves the number.
foods.summary: A communal hotpot where the calories swing wildly depending on your broth, protein choices, and whether you ordered noodles or not.
foods.answer: A typical Malaysian steamboat sitting comes in at around 750 calories per person, based on a 650g mix of sliced meats, seafood, noodles, veg, and clear broth with dipping sauce. That figure covers the standard hawker version: a bit of everything in a clear chicken or pork bone broth. Go mala and you are looking at 1,200 calories easy, because the soup base alone is basically chilli oil and lard. Stick to clear broth with lean protein and skip the noodles and you can get it down to 400 calories for the same satisfying meal.
realTalk: Steamboat is one of those meals that feels healthy because you are cooking everything in hot water, but the number can surprise you. The baseline estimate is around 750 calories per person for a standard mixed plate in clear broth, and that is genuinely a decent meal: 48g of protein, 65g of carbs, reasonable fat. The catch is that this is a rough ballpark. Hard data on steamboat is thin because every table orders differently, every shop uses a different recipe, and nobody is weighing their prawns at a steamboat restaurant. So treat 750 as a reasonable middle ground, not a lab result.

What actually moves the number is the broth and the processed stuff. Mala broth can add 400 to 600 calories on its own before you put a single prawn in the pot. The processed items like fish balls, tofu puffs, and crabsticks are sneaky too, about 110 calories in just 60g because they are made with starch and oil. Noodles add another 210 calories for 60g dry weight. If you want to keep steamboat under 500 calories, the formula is simple: clear broth, lean chicken or seafood only, load up the veg (150g of cabbage and mushrooms is only 60 calories), and skip the noodles. You will still leave the table full, bro.
lighter: Pick clear chicken or pork bone broth, not mala, tom yam, or creamy broth. The broth base alone is the biggest calorie lever at this table.
Skip the noodles or take half a portion. Going from 60g dry noodles to nothing saves you 210 calories without you even noticing once the table is full of everything else.
Limit processed items like fish balls, tofu puffs, and crabsticks. They are calorie-dense for their size. Load your plate with raw veg instead.
Go heavy on prawns, sliced chicken, and fish over pork belly and fatty beef slices. Lean protein fills you up and costs less in fat calories.
Watch the dipping sauce. A small dish of sesame paste or peanut sauce can add 80 to 150 calories without you realising it. Use light soy sauce with chilli instead.

faq.q: How many calories in Steamboat?
faq.a: A standard Malaysian steamboat serving comes in at around 750 calories per person, based on a 650g mix of meats, seafood, noodles, veg, and clear broth. A light version with no noodles and clear broth drops to about 400 calories, while a mala broth version can hit 1,200 calories.

faq.q: Is steamboat good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can be, if you control the variables. Clear broth, lean protein, lots of veg, and no noodles gets you a filling 400-calorie meal with decent protein. The problem is most people also order pork belly, processed fish balls, noodles, and a creamy or mala broth. That combination pushes you past 1,000 calories pretty fast.

faq.q: Why is mala steamboat so high in calories?
faq.a: The mala soup base is essentially chilli oil, lard, and spices. Before a single piece of meat hits the pot, that base can add 400 to 600 calories per person. If you share the pot with one other person the impact is lower, but solo mala diners are basically drinking flavoured oil throughout the meal.

foods.name: Ayam Percik
foods.metaDescription: Ayam Percik has around 360 calories per thigh piece with sauce. Here's what's actually driving those numbers and how to order smart at the stall.
foods.summary: Grilled chicken coated in spiced coconut sauce from the east coast, 360 calories per thigh piece and genuinely one of the more protein-friendly lauk options at the stall.
foods.answer: One piece of Ayam Percik (a thigh, bone-in, with the percik sauce) comes in at around 360 calories. That's 32g protein, 21g fat, and 10g carbs for a 220g serving. Not a bad trade for how satisfying it is, honestly. The coconut-based percik sauce adds most of the fat, but the chicken itself is doing real work on the protein front. Fair deal.
realTalk: Ayam Percik is genuinely one of the better lauk options if you are watching your calories, and that surprises a lot of people. You get 360 calories and 32g of protein in a single piece, which is a pretty solid ratio. The main drivers here are the percik sauce, made with santan, palm sugar, and spices, and the chicken thigh skin. Without those two things this dish would be quite lean. With them, you get that rich sticky glaze that makes Ayam Percik worth travelling to Kelantan for. Honest caveat though: the numbers on this page are a genuine ballpark estimate. Hard nutritional data for traditional kampung-style Ayam Percik is basically nonexistent, and every mak cik's recipe is different. Treat 360 as your working number, not gospel.

What actually changes the maths is which piece you order and how sauce-heavy the stall is. A drumstick runs about 290 calories versus 360 for a thigh, so if you are at a buffet or a festival stall and want two pieces, go for the two kaki option instead of one peha and save yourself 70 calories. The half chicken serving at about 700 calories is really a sharing portion, bro, not a solo meal. At home, if you swap full-fat santan for the light version in the percik sauce, you can probably shave 30 to 40 calories off the sauce portion without destroying the flavour. The protein is the star here. 32g from one piece is excellent for a lauk, easily on par with ayam bakar, and it keeps you full enough to not raid the kuih tray afterward.
lighter: Order the drumstick instead of the thigh and you save about 70 calories per piece.
Ask for less sauce or eat around the heaviest glaze patches, the percik coating is where most of the fat lives.
Skip the skin. Yes it tastes good. But the skin on one thigh adds a noticeable chunk of fat and maybe 40-50 calories.
Pair it with plain white rice or nasi kerabu instead of nasi lemak or nasi minyak. Your side dishes matter.
If you are cooking at home, use light coconut milk for the percik sauce. The flavour difference is smaller than you think, and the calorie difference is real.

faq.a: One standard piece (chicken thigh with percik sauce) is around 360 calories. A drumstick drops to about 290 calories, while a half chicken serving can hit 700 calories.

faq.q: Is Ayam Percik good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can fit into a weight loss diet. The chicken thigh gives you 32g of protein which keeps you full, and 360 calories for a main is totally manageable. The issue is portion size, how thick the sauce coating is, and what you pair it with. Eat it with plain rice and some vegetables and you have a solid meal.

faq.q: What makes Ayam Percik so high in fat?
faq.a: Two things: chicken thigh skin, and the percik sauce made with santan (coconut milk). The skin alone contributes a chunk of the fat, and coconut milk is naturally high in saturated fat. Drumstick has slightly less, but you cannot really get away from the sauce if you want authentic Ayam Percik.

foods.name: Ayam Bakar
foods.metaDescription: Ayam bakar has 290 calories per piece (thigh or drumstick, 170g). See how madu vs berempah changes the count, and tips to keep it lighter.
foods.summary: Grilled marinated chicken, a warung staple, and one of the better calorie-to-protein deals in Malaysian lauk if you pick the right version.
foods.answer: One piece of ayam bakar (a thigh or drumstick quarter, about 170g) comes in at 290 calories, with 28g protein, 6g carbs, and 16g fat. That number covers the grilled chicken with skin plus the marinade. It is honestly one of the better lauk options at the warung if you are watching your intake, because you are getting solid protein without the calorie count going completely out of hand.
realTalk: Ayam bakar is genuinely one of the more diet-friendly things you can pick off a nasi campur counter, which is not something you can say about most Malaysian lauk. At 290 calories for a whole piece of thigh or drumstick, you are getting 28g of protein for that spend. The calories mostly come from the chicken itself with skin (245 cal) and the marinade adds about 45 calories on top. Where things go sideways is the madu version. That honey glaze is not a small difference, it pushes a piece up to 330 calories and bumps your carbs noticeably. Berempah sits in the middle at 300 calories because the rempah paste adds a bit of oil. So the version matters, but none of them are disaster territory lah.

What actually changes the maths is three things: version, skin, and what you eat with it. Biasa saves you 10 to 50 calories versus berempah or madu. Removing the skin before eating knocks off roughly 40 to 60 calories. And the rice underneath is the real wildcard, 200g of white rice is already 260 calories before you even touch the chicken. If you are eating ayam bakar at a warung and wondering why you are not losing weight, the honest answer is probably not the ayam. It is the rice, the sambal, and the kuah that come with it. Keep the chicken, manage the sides.
lighter: Skip the madu version. Ayam bakar madu clocks in at 330 calories versus 280 for the plain biasa, purely because of the honey glaze sugar.

Remove the skin before eating. Most of the protein is in the meat, and you still get plenty of the marinade flavour from the flesh itself, so you are not eating cardboard. Dropping the skin saves you 40 to 60 calories per piece.
Watch your nasi. The ayam itself is fine. It is the mountain of rice underneath that wrecks the meal. Keep rice to 150 to 180g cooked.
Pair it with ulam or kangkung belacan instead of a heavy gravy side. Gravy is where hidden calories creep in.
Ask for the chicken without the extra sambal drizzled on top at the warung counter. That sambal can add another 30 to 60 calories depending on how heavy-handed the aunty is.

faq.q: How many calories in Ayam Bakar?
faq.a: One standard piece (thigh or drumstick quarter, about 170g) has 290 calories. That includes the grilled chicken with skin and the marinade. Ayam bakar madu (honey glaze) pushes it up to around 330 calories per piece because of the added sugar.

faq.q: Is ayam bakar good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can be, yes. At 290 calories with 28g of protein per piece, it is one of the leaner lauk options at a nasi campur or warung counter. The main thing to watch is the marinade sugar, especially the madu version. Stick to biasa or berempah and pair it with plain rice or ulam instead of nasi lemak and you are in decent shape.

faq.q: Does removing the skin reduce calories significantly?
faq.a: Yes, a fair bit. The skin on a thigh or drumstick adds roughly 40 to 60 calories depending on size. If you are being careful, removing the skin before eating drops you closer to 230 to 250 calories per piece and cuts the fat noticeably.

foods.name: Daging Dendeng
foods.metaDescription: Daging Dendeng has about 330 calories per serving. The beef is solid protein but frying oil adds up fast. Here's what you're actually eating.
foods.summary: Thin, crispy spiced beef slices cooked Minang style, often served with sambal, packing more calories than the small portion suggests.
foods.answer: Daging Dendeng comes in at around 330 calories per serving of 3-4 thin slices (about 90g). The beef itself only accounts for roughly 185 kcal, but the frying oil absorbed during cooking adds another 100 kcal on top. So yeah, this is one of those dishes that looks small but hits harder than you expect calorie-wise.
realTalk: 330 calories for 3-4 thin slices of beef sounds reasonable until you realise those slices weigh maybe 90g total and a third of the calories (100 kcal) is literally just absorbed frying oil. The beef itself is actually decent protein, 24g per serving, which is solid. But dendeng is one of those deceptive lauk items where you see a small pile of meat and think you're being good, then you grab another serving without thinking. Worth noting this is a ballpark estimate as hard calorie data for dendeng specifically is thin, so treat 330 kcal as a useful working number rather than a precise lab result.

What really moves the number is how the beef was cooked and how much sambal they pile on. Standard crispy fried dendeng (the plain version without extra sambal topping) is where you get the 330 kcal base. Dendeng balado is specifically the crispy version dressed with a balado red chili sambal on top, which pushes it closer to 350 kcal. The dendeng lambok, the softer moist style, drops down to around 280 kcal because less oil is absorbed. Portion control is where most people slip up lah, because dendeng goes so well with plain rice that you just keep reaching. If you can stick to one serving (those 3-4 slices) and pair it with a big scoop of veg instead of extra rice, the protein-to-calorie ratio is actually pretty decent for a lauk option.
lighter: Ask for dendeng lambok instead of the crispy fried version, you save about 50 calories per serving just from less oil absorption.
Eat it with plain white rice rather than nasi lemak or nasi goreng, the lauk is already doing work so keep the base simple.
One serving is 3-4 slices, not the whole plate. Pair it with a big portion of kangkung or ulam to fill up without adding much to your calorie total.
Go easy on extra sambal topping. The sambal adds 20 kcal per serving and it is easy to double that at a nasi campur counter.
At a nasi campur place, take dendeng as your protein pick but skip the other fried lauk alongside it, do not double up on the oily stuff.

faq.q: How many calories in Daging Dendeng?
faq.a: A standard serving of daging dendeng, about 3-4 thin slices totalling 90g, comes to around 330 calories. The beef contributes 185 kcal and absorbed frying oil accounts for another 100 kcal.

faq.q: Is daging dendeng good for a diet?
faq.a: It is a reasonable protein source at 24g protein per serving, but the 22g of fat from deep frying means the calories stack up quickly. If you can get the moist dendeng lambok style instead, you drop to around 280 kcal. One serving with vegetables and plain rice works fine in a calorie deficit.

faq.q: What is the difference between dendeng balado and dendeng lambok?

foods.name: Daging Harimau Menangis
foods.serving: 1 hawker plate (grilled beef slices with dipping sauce)
foods.metaDescription: Daging Harimau Menangis has around 630 calories per hawker plate. Here's what's driving the numbers and how to eat it without wrecking your deficit.
foods.summary: Grilled beef slices with a punchy chilli-soy-lime dip, where most of the calories live in the cut of beef, not the sauce.
foods.answer: A hawker plate of Daging Harimau Menangis comes in at around 630 calories for a standard 230g serving of grilled beef slices with the chilli-soy-lime dipping sauce. The bulk of that, about 540 calories, is coming straight from the beef itself (roughly 200g of grilled brisket or batang pinang). The marinade adds another 50 and the dipping sauce is practically free at 40. So yeah, 630 calories for what is honestly a pretty satisfying plate of grilled beef. Not bad at all if you are tracking.
realTalk: 630 calories for a plate of grilled beef is honestly pretty reasonable, bro. You are getting 50g of protein out of it, which is solid. The issue is the fat, 38g, and that comes entirely from the beef cut. Batang pinang and brisket have decent fat marbling, and when it gets grilled and then soaked in a kicap manis marinade with brown sugar, those calories stack up fast. The dipping sauce is basically nothing calorie-wise, 40 calories for 30g of chilli-soy-lime, so do not stress about it. Worth flagging that these numbers are a ballpark estimate because there is very little hard calorie data published specifically for this dish, so treat 630 as a reasonable working figure, not a precise lab reading.

What actually moves the number is the cut of beef and how big the portion is. If the uncle uses a fattier brisket or gives you a generous 300g plate, you are looking at closer to 850 calories. Swap to a leaner cut like tenderloin with a lighter marinade and you drop to around 480. The marinade itself adds about 50 calories from the oyster sauce, kicap manis and sugar absorbed into the meat, so asking for less marinade or a drier grill does help a bit. Paired with plain rice this becomes a complete meal, but watch the rice portion because that is where most people accidentally eat another 300-400 calories without thinking lah.
lighter: Ask for a leaner cut like sirloin or tenderloin instead of brisket, drops you from 630 to around 480 calories.
Request less marinade or a drier grill finish to cut the kicap manis and brown sugar contribution, saves maybe 20-30 calories.
The dipping sauce is already basically free at 40 calories, so dip away freely and don't stress that part.
Control your rice portion on the side. A standard scoop of white rice is 200-250 calories on its own, that is where most of the meal's total goes.
Eat this as your main protein with plain rice and a vegetable side, it is a genuinely high-protein option at 50g per plate.

faq.q: Is Daging Harimau Menangis good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can work, actually. At 630 calories and 50g of protein, the protein-to-calorie ratio is decent. The main thing to manage is the cut of beef (leaner is better) and what you eat with it. foods.name: Sambal Sotong
foods.metaDescription: Sambal sotong has around 270 calories per lauk serving. High protein, moderate fat from the sambal. Here's what's actually in it and how to order smarter.
foods.summary: Squid cooked in sambal tumis, a classic Malaysian lauk that's surprisingly decent protein for the calories if you watch the sauce.
foods.answer: Sambal sotong comes in at around 270 calories for a standard lauk serving of about 200g. That's roughly 130g of cooked squid with a decent scoop of sambal tumis on top. The squid itself is actually pretty lean at around 130 calories, but the sambal sauce (chilli, oil, onion, belacan) adds another 110 calories on top of that. So yeah, it's not the heaviest dish on the table, but the sauce does most of the calorie work here.
realTalk: Sambal sotong is honestly one of the better lauk options if you're watching calories, bro. A standard hawker serving sits at around 270 calories for 200g, and 28g of protein is solid for a side dish. The squid itself is lean, maybe 130 calories for 130g cooked. The rest comes from the sambal tumis, which is where the oil, chilli paste, and belacan gang up on you for about 110 calories. Add petai and you're looking at 310 calories instead. None of these are scary numbers on their own, but fair warning: these are ballpark estimates. Hard calorie data for Malaysian home-cooked and hawker dishes is thin, so treat this as a reasonable guide rather than a lab result.

What actually changes the maths is the sambal. A generous auntie at the nasi campur stall who drowns your sotong in sauce can easily push your 270-calorie serving toward 350 or higher. Ask for less gravy or scoop the squid pieces and leave some sauce behind. On the flip end, sotong bakar (grilled squid with sambal on the side) drops to around 220 calories because you skip the oil absorption from wet cooking. Sotong goreng kunyit goes the other way, up to about 330 calories because deep-frying pulls in more oil than a wet sambal does. The squid itself is doing you a favour with the protein. The cooking method and sauce quantity are what decide whether this is a smart pick or not.
lighter: Go for sotong bakar if available, grilled squid with sambal on the side comes in at around 220 calories instead of 270.
At nasi campur, ask for less sambal gravy and more of the squid pieces. The sauce is where most of the fat lives.
Skip the petai if you're being strict. It adds roughly 30 to 40 calories and you probably won't miss it on a deficit day.
Pair it with plain rice and a veg side instead of nasi lemak or nasi goreng. The sotong is already flavourful enough that you don't need a fancy base.
Watch your total lauk count. Sambal sotong at 270 calories is fine as your one main lauk, but if you're stacking it with rendang and sambal udang on the same plate, the calories add up fast lah.

faq.a: A standard lauk serving of sambal sotong (about 200g) has around 270 calories, with 28g protein, 10g carbs, and 12g fat. The squid contributes roughly 130 calories and the sambal tumis sauce adds another 110 or so.

faq.q: Is sambal sotong good for weight loss?
faq.a: It can be, actually. The squid is a lean protein and 270 calories for a lauk isn't bad at all. The thing to watch is the sambal sauce, which carries most of the fat. Ask for less gravy, or go for sotong bakar at around 220 calories if you want the lower-calorie version.

faq.q: How does sambal sotong compare to sambal udang in calories?
faq.a: They're in a similar range. Prawns and squid are both lean seafood, so the calorie difference mostly comes down to the sambal quantity and whether extra ingredients like petai are added. Sambal sotong at 270 calories is a reasonable benchmark for either dish.

foods.name: Sambal Udang
foods.metaDescription: Sambal Udang is around 300 calories for a hawker plate of 8-10 prawns. Here's what drives the numbers and how to order smarter.
foods.summary: Spicy sambal-coated prawns, a staple lauk at any nasi campur counter, where the prawns are lean but the oil in the sambal does most of the calorie work.
foods.answer: Sambal Udang at a hawker stall comes in at around 300 calories for a standard plate of 8-10 medium prawns. The prawns themselves are only about 115 calories, but the sambal paste and cooking oil push the total up to 300 kcal. Not bad for a lauk, actually, considering you're getting 22g of protein out of it.
realTalk: Sambal Udang is actually one of the better lauk options at the nasi campur counter, bro. A full hawker plate sits around 300 calories, which sounds okay until you realise that most of those calories, about 160 of them, come from the cooking oil alone. The prawns are 115 kcal, the sambal paste is only 20 kcal. So the dish itself is not the problem; it's the wok technique and how heavy-handed the cook is with the oil. To be honest, these are ballpark estimates because there's basically no solid published calorie data for Malaysian hawker sambal udang. Different cooks, different oil amounts, different prawn sizes. Take the 300 figure as a reasonable middle ground, not a hard measurement.

The thing that really changes the maths is portion size and how much gravy you take. A small nasi campur scoop can be as low as 190 calories if you get a lighter ladle. Ask the aunty for 'kurang kuah' and you drop maybe 40 to 60 kcal straight away. On the other end, if you go butter prawn or cereal prawn, you're looking at 420 calories because those are deep-fried in batter with a butter-egg coating. Udang goreng tepung is even worse at 480 calories due to the batter absorbing oil. Stick to sambal and you keep the protein-to-calorie ratio decent, 22g protein at 300 kcal is genuinely not bad for a lauk.
lighter: Ask for less sambal gravy at nasi campur, you can shave off 30 to 50 calories just by reducing the oil-heavy sauce.
Order the small nasi campur scoop instead of a full plate, that drops you from 300 to around 190 calories.
Skip the butter prawn or cereal prawn versions, those are 420-480 calories and the frying adds a lot of fat fast.
Shell-on prawns mean you naturally eat slower and feel fuller on less, so embrace the peeling process.
If you cook at home, use a non-stick pan and measure your oil to 1 teaspoon instead of eyeballing it from the bottle.

faq.q: Is Sambal Udang good for weight loss?

foods.name: Ikan Bakar

foods.metaDescription: Ikan bakar is about 300 calories per hawker portion with 38g protein. Here's what's actually in it and how to order smart.
foods.summary: Grilled fish wrapped in banana leaf with sambal or percik, one of the leanest lauk options at the warung if you know what to order.
foods.answer: Ikan bakar comes in at around 300 calories for a standard hawker portion, which is one piece of grilled fish with sambal coating, roughly 220g total. That's about 175g of edible fish meat giving you 175 calories, plus 55 calories from the sambal marinade, and around 70 calories from oil absorbed during grilling. For a proper lauk dish this is actually pretty decent, especially when you consider you're getting 38g of protein out of it.
realTalk: Ikan bakar is genuinely one of the better things you can eat at a warung, and 300 calories for a full piece of grilled fish with sambal is not bad at all. The fish itself is doing a lot of the heavy lifting here, around 175 calories for 175g of lean white or semi-oily fish flesh, and you're walking away with 38g of protein. The sambal coating adds about 55 calories and the grilling oil adds another 70. To be honest, these are ballpark estimates because there's almost no hard nutritional data on Malaysian hawker ikan bakar specifically, the fish species varies, the marinade recipe is different at every stall, and how much oil gets absorbed depends on the grill. Treat these numbers as a reasonable middle ground, not gospel. But directionally, this is a lean high-protein dish and you should be eating it more often.

What actually moves the numbers is the sauce and the fish type. Plain ikan kembung bakar with just turmeric and no sambal? That's closer to 200 calories. The moment you go percik style with santan in the sauce, you're looking at 380 calories for the same-ish portion, that coconut milk adds up fast. Petai on the side only bumps you 30-50 calories extra which is nothing. The oil absorbed during grilling is the silent killer that people forget, a heavily basted fish can absorb significantly more than the 8g we're estimating here. So the practical move is ask for less sambal paste, skip the percik if you're cutting, and pair it with plain rice and ulam instead of nasi lemak. You keep the protein, lose the unnecessary calories.
lighter: Order ikan kembung bakar with turmeric only, no thick sambal paste, drops the count to around 200 calories.
Ask the uncle to go easy on the oil basting during grilling, a drier grill means less absorbed fat.
Skip the percik sauce version when you're cutting, the santan alone adds roughly 80 extra calories.
Pair with plain white rice and ulam-ulaman instead of nasi lemak or heavy gravies alongside.
If you're adding petai, that's fine, only 30-50 calories extra and the fibre helps you stay full.

faq.q: Is ikan bakar good for weight loss?

foods.name: Ikan Masak Lemak
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Masak Lemak has around 370 calories per hawker serving. The fish is lean, but that santan gravy does serious work. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Fish cooked in a rich coconut milk and turmeric gravy, a staple at any nasi campur counter where the santan is doing most of the calorie heavy lifting.
foods.answer: One hawker portion of Ikan Masak Lemak (fish plus gravy, around 220g) comes in at roughly 370 calories. The fish itself is only about 140 calories, but that coconut milk gravy adds another 175 calories on top, which is where most of the damage comes from. High fat at 27g, decent protein at 24g, low carbs at 7g. Eat it with a plate of white rice and you are looking at 600 to 700 calories total depending on the rice portion.
realTalk: Honestly, 370 calories for a lauk portion is not that bad on its own. The fish itself, maybe 130g of ikan merah or tenggiri, is only around 140 calories and gives you a solid 24g of protein. The problem is the gravy. That 70g of santan-based kuah is packing 175 calories, more than the actual fish, and it soaks into everything on your plate. Worth flagging that these are ballpark estimates, because hard nutrition data for Malaysian home-style and hawker dishes is basically nonexistent. The real number could be 330 or it could be 420 depending on how heavy-handed the cook is with the coconut milk that day.

What actually moves the maths is how much gravy you take and whether the cook uses thick santan or the thinner stuff. A Negeri Sembilan-style masak lemak cili api version with extra santan can push to 430 calories for the same size portion. If you get kembong instead of a bigger fillet, the whole thing drops to around 280 calories because the portion is smaller and there is less gravy per serving. Practically speaking, if you are watching calories, ask for less kuah, eat the fish and leave some gravy in the tray. You can easily shave 50 to 80 calories just doing that, and you still get most of the flavour lah.
lighter: Ask the nasi campur auntie for less gravy, or scoop the fish out first before adding gravy yourself. The kuah is 175 calories of that 370.
Choose ikan kembong (mackerel) over bigger fillet options. Smaller portion, leaner fish, less gravy, whole thing comes to around 280 calories.
Pair with plain steamed vegetables instead of another santan-based lauk. One heavy coconut dish per meal is enough.
Go for ikan bakar or ikan masak asam pedas on the days when you want fish but want to skip the santan entirely. Saves you 150 to 200 calories easy.
Do not scoop up the remaining gravy to eat with rice. That pooled kuah at the bottom of your plate is basically concentrated calories with no protein to show for it.

faq.q: Is Ikan Masak Lemak healthy for weight loss?

foods.name: Ikan Patin Masak Tempoyak
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Patin Masak Tempoyak has about 380 calories per restaurant piece with gravy. Here's what's driving that number and how to eat it smarter.
foods.summary: Patin fish cooked in fermented durian and coconut gravy, a Pahang classic that tastes incredible but comes with a fat bill you should know about.
foods.answer: Ikan Patin Masak Tempoyak comes in at around 380 calories for a standard hawker or restaurant portion, which is one piece of patin fish (about 150g cooked) with gravy, weighing roughly 280g total. That calorie count is spread across 23g protein, 10g carbs, and 20g fat. Not a light dish by any means, but also not a disaster if you eat it with plain rice and skip the extra ladle of gravy.
realTalk: 380 calories for one piece of fish sounds reasonable until you remember that patin is a naturally fatty river fish, and then you pile on tempoyak (fermented durian, which is basically concentrated durian fat and sugar) plus coconut milk in the gravy. The 90 calories from coconut milk alone and 68 from the tempoyak paste add up fast. To be honest, the numbers here are a ballpark estimate because solid nutritional data for this dish is basically nonexistent. Patin's fat content varies depending on the fish size and season, and every mak cik recipes the tempoyak ratio differently. Treat 380 calories as a reasonable middle-ground guess, not a lab result.

What actually moves the number is how much gravy ends up on your plate. That thick, lemak gravy is where most of the calories hide. If you ask for less gravy, or go with the tanpa santan version (broth-based, no coconut milk), you can bring it down to around 250 calories. The heavy gulai-style version with a thick coconut curry base goes up to about 460 calories for the same size piece. The fish itself is only around 175 calories for 150g, so the protein is actually decent, bro. If you pair one piece with a smaller portion of rice and load up on vegetables instead, the full meal can stay under 600 calories without feeling like punishment.
lighter: Ask for kurang gravy when ordering, the thick tempoyak-santan gravy is where most of the calories are hiding.
Go for the tanpa santan version if the stall offers it, that alone saves you about 130 calories.
Pair it with extra vegetables like kangkung or ulam instead of a second scoop of rice.
One piece is enough as your lauk, do not order two pieces thinking it is a light fish dish.
Eat the fish, leave behind any excess pooled gravy on the plate, that last tablespoon is probably another 30 to 50 calories of coconut oil.

faq.q: Is patin fish high in fat?
faq.a: Yes, patin (pangasius) is a naturally fatty river fish compared to leaner options like tilapia or siakap. That fat is part of why it tastes so good in tempoyak gravy, but it does mean the calories add up faster than you might expect for a fish dish.

faq.q: Can I eat Ikan Patin Masak Tempoyak while on a diet?
faq.a: Yes, one piece is manageable at 380 calories as long as you watch the rest of your meal. Keep the rice portion small, go easy on extra gravy, and load up on vegetables on the side. The 23g of protein is actually solid for staying full.
