faq.q: How many calories in Kek Lapis Sarawak?
faq.a: One standard slice of Kek Lapis Sarawak (45g) is about 200 calories. The number shifts depending on the variant: plain or pandan sits around 200 to 205, cheese filling bumps it to 250, and durian filling goes up to 270 calories per slice.

faq.q: What actually is Kek Lapis Sarawak?
faq.a: It's a layered cake from Sarawak where each coloured band is baked individually, layer by layer, until you get a dense striped loaf. The batter is loaded with butter, whole eggs, condensed milk and sugar, which is why it's so rich. It's a prestige gift item, especially during Gawai and Hari Raya, and a serious point of Sarawakian pride.

faq.q: Is Kek Lapis Sarawak healthy?
faq.a: Straightforwardly, no. It's a celebration cake built almost entirely on butter, eggs and sugar. At 200 calories for a 45g slice with 12g fat, it's calorie dense without offering much protein or fibre in return. That's not a reason to never eat it, it's just not an everyday snack if you're watching your intake.

foods.name: Khau Yuk
foods.serving: 1 serving (3-4 slices pork belly with mui choy and gravy)
foods.metaDescription: Khau Yuk (Hakka braised pork belly) has around 490 calories per serving. Most of it is fat from the pork belly. Here is what you are actually eating.
foods.summary: Khau Yuk is a Hakka braised pork belly dish, slow-cooked with preserved mustard greens (mui choy) or fermented bean curd until the fat is meltingly soft.
foods.answer: A standard serving of Khau Yuk, which is 3 to 4 slices of braised pork belly with mui choy and gravy (about 220g total), comes in at around 490 calories. That is 16g protein, 8g carbs, and a hefty 41g of fat. This is Hakka braised pork belly, slow-cooked until the skin and fat layers go completely soft, and those numbers do not lie about where the calories are coming from.
realTalk: Khau Yuk is a Hakka dish you will find at kopitiams and Chinese restaurants across Malaysia, especially in communities with strong Hakka roots. The dish is pork belly braised low and slow with either mui choy (preserved mustard greens) or nam yue (red fermented bean curd), sometimes with fried taro layered in between. The result is pork belly so soft the fat practically dissolves when you eat it. That melt-in-your-mouth texture is exactly why 100g of the pork belly alone clocks in at 395 calories. The mui choy adds almost nothing calorie-wise at just 18 calories per 60g, but the braising sauce and absorbed oil contribute another 77 calories. So 490 calories for a serving is a reasonable ballpark, though be honest: this is a genuine estimate. Hard nutritional data for home-style Hakka dishes like this is thin, and fat content can swing quite a bit depending on how thick the belly slices are and how generously the cook ladles on the gravy.

The biggest variable here is portion size and how much gravy you take. Khau Yuk is not a lean protein situation, full stop. If you are counting calories, the practical move is to eat one or two slices instead of three or four, which cuts you from 490 calories down to roughly 250 to 300 calories. Skip the extra ladle of braising sauce too, that alone saves you maybe 30 to 40 calories per tablespoon of oil-rich gravy. The taro version (wu tau kau yuk) jumps to around 640 calories because deep-fried taro absorbs a lot of oil, so if you are watching numbers, stick to the mui choy version. Pair it with plain steamed rice rather than claypot or fried rice to keep the overall meal from blowing out your deficit for the day.
lighter: Take two slices instead of three or four. That alone brings you from 490 calories down to roughly 250 calories.
Ask for less gravy or leave the pooled oil at the bottom of the dish. The braising oil is where a chunk of the fat calories hide.
Go for the mui choy version over the taro version. Wu tau kau yuk is about 640 calories because of the fried taro, so the mustard greens version saves you roughly 150 calories per serving.
Eat it with plain steamed rice, not fried rice. Khau Yuk on white rice is already a full meal without adding another 400 calories from the rice side.
Balance the plate with a simple stir-fried vegetable like kangkung or kailan to pad the volume without adding much to your calorie count.

variants.name: Mui choy (preserved mustard greens) version
variants.note: Most common in Malaysian kopitiams and Hakka restaurants; mustard greens add negligible calories

variants.name: Nam yue (red fermented bean curd) version without taro
variants.note: Richer sauce from fermented bean curd adds slightly more fat and sodium

variants.name: Wu tau kau yuk (with fried taro)
variants.note: Deep-fried taro slices interleaved with pork belly add ~120-150 kcal from starch and absorbed frying oil

faq.q: How many calories in Khau Yuk?
faq.a: A standard serving of Khau Yuk (3 to 4 slices pork belly with mui choy and gravy, about 220g) is around 490 calories, with 16g protein, 8g carbs, and 41g fat. Note that this is a ballpark estimate as detailed nutrition data for this dish is not widely available.

faq.q: What exactly is Khau Yuk?
faq.a: Khau Yuk is a Hakka braised pork belly dish. The pork belly is slow-braised with either mui choy (preserved mustard greens) or nam yue (red fermented bean curd) until the fat layers go completely soft. It is a non-halal dish and one of the classic comfort foods in Malaysian Chinese cooking.

faq.q: Is Khau Yuk healthy?
faq.a: Honestly, no, not if you are trying to lose weight. At 490 calories for a small serving and 41g of fat, it is one of the higher-calorie lauk options out there. It is not something to eat every day if you are in a deficit. That said, a couple of slices alongside vegetables and plain rice is manageable as an occasional meal, just keep your portion honest.

foods.name: Abacus Seeds
foods.metaDescription: Abacus Seeds clock in at around 520 calories per plate. Here's what's actually in that chewy Hakka yam-dough dish and whether it fits your goals.
foods.summary: A Hakka stir-fried dish of chewy yam-tapioca dough beads tossed with minced pork, dried shrimp, mushroom and black fungus, popular in Hakka communities across Malaysia.
foods.answer: One plate of Abacus Seeds (around 320g) comes in at roughly 520 calories, with 22g protein, 65g carbs and 18g fat. The yam-tapioca dough beads carry most of the carb load, while the minced pork and cooking oil push the fat and protein up. Fair warning, these numbers are a ballpark estimate since hard nutritional data for this dish is basically nonexistent, but 500-plus calories for a full plate is a reasonable working figure.
realTalk: Abacus Seeds (算盘子, suan pan zi) is a Hakka dish you'll find at Hakka restaurants and some heritage kopitiam spots across Malaysia, especially in KL, Bentong and parts of Sabah. If you've never had it, the dough beads are made from yam and tapioca starch, then hand-rolled into little round shapes that look like abacus beads, boiled and stir-fried with minced pork, dried shrimp, shiitake mushrooms and black fungus. The texture is QQ and slightly sticky, think a chewier version of mochi but savory. At 520 calories a plate it's not a diet food, but it's also not a disaster. The yam dough beads alone account for 290 of those calories, and the minced pork adds another 145. To be straight with you though, this is a medium-confidence estimate because proper lab-tested nutrition data for Abacus Seeds is basically nonexistent. Take the number as a useful guide, not gospel.

What actually moves the number is how heavy-handed the wok is with oil and how big the portion is. A generous cook who doubles the oil can easily add 80 to 100 extra calories without you noticing. Portion size is the other big lever: a smaller serve of 200g instead of 320g would drop you closer to 325 calories. The minced pork contributes real protein but also fat, so if you could swap in lean chicken mince you'd save maybe 30 to 40 calories. Ask for less oil if you're ordering at a restaurant, most places will accommodate. The dried shrimp and mushrooms are practically free at only 40 calories for 30g, so don't stress about those.
lighter: Ask for less oil at the wok. This dish traditionally uses a fair bit and even cutting it by half saves you around 40 to 60 calories.
Eat a smaller portion. 200g instead of 320g puts you around 325 calories and honestly still feels satisfying because the dough is dense and chewy.
Pair it with a clear soup or a plate of stir-fried sayur manis instead of ordering extra rice or another fried item.
Skip any extra sauce or gravy that some places pour over. That stuff adds calories fast and you can't easily account for it.
Share a plate between two people and bulk up with a simple vegetable dish on the side. You still get to enjoy the flavour without eating the full 520 calories yourself.

faq.q: How many calories in Abacus Seeds?
faq.a: One plate of Abacus Seeds (roughly 320g) is around 520 calories. That breaks down to about 22g protein, 65g carbs and 18g fat. This is a solid estimate but hard to pin down precisely since the dish doesn't have much published nutritional data.

faq.q: What exactly are Abacus Seeds?
faq.a: Abacus Seeds are a Hakka dish made from yam and tapioca starch dough that's hand-shaped into little bead-like rounds, boiled until chewy, then stir-fried with minced pork, dried shrimp, mushrooms and black fungus. They taste savory and slightly earthy from the yam, with a QQ chewy bite. It's not pork-free, so non-halal.

faq.q: Is Abacus Seeds healthy?
faq.a: It's a balanced enough meal with decent protein from the pork and reasonable carbs from the yam dough, but 520 calories a plate means it's not a light option. The bigger issue is the oil used in stir-frying, which you can't always control. If you're counting calories, treat it as a proper meal rather than a snack, and maybe skip the sugary drink that usually comes with it.

foods.name: Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken)
foods.serving: 1 serving (2-3 bone-in chicken pieces with wine sauce)
foods.metaDescription: Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken) has around 530 calories per serving. The sesame oil is what pushes the number up. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: A Foochow-Sarawak classic from Sibu where chicken is braised in red glutinous rice wine and sesame oil, traditionally served during confinement but honestly too good to wait that long.
foods.answer: One serving of Ayam Masak Arak, which is 2 to 3 bone-in pieces with the wine sauce, comes in at around 530 calories, with 30g protein, 6g carbs, and 35g fat. The dish is lower carb than you'd expect but the fat is real because sesame oil alone contributes about 180 calories per serving. These are honest estimates since detailed nutritional data for this dish is sparse, so treat it as a ballpark rather than a precise lab result.
realTalk: Ayam Masak Arak is a Foochow confinement dish from Sibu, Sarawak. If you're not from that community, you may have only seen it at Sarawakian kopitiam or at a friend's mum's place after she gave birth. It's chicken braised in ang chao, which is red glutinous rice wine, cooked down with sesame oil and ginger until the sauce is fragrant and slightly sticky. At 530 calories for a solid serving, it's not a diet dish. The two big calorie drivers are the sesame oil, about 180 calories from just 1.5 tablespoons, and the chicken thigh and drumstick fat. On the protein side, 30g is decent. Worth flagging: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for this dish basically doesn't exist, so there's genuine uncertainty of maybe plus or minus 60 to 80 calories per serving.

What actually moves the number is mostly the oil. A soup-style version with more wine broth and less sesame oil drops the count to around 380 calories for the chicken and broth alone. The rich confinement version with extra sesame oil and wine can hit 680 calories for the same portion size. If you're eating it at home or at a kopitiam, ask for less oil in the braising if you can. Choosing breast over thigh would cut maybe 40 to 60 calories from the chicken portion. The ang chao wine and dregs themselves only add about 75 calories from the 70g in a standard serving, so the wine isn't the villain here.
lighter: Ask for the soup-style version with more wine broth and less sesame oil. That alone can bring it down to around 380 calories.
Skip the mee sua noodles if they come on the side. They add calories fast and you probably don't need them if you're already eating rice.
If you're cooking at home, cut the sesame oil to 1 tablespoon instead of 1.5. You still get the flavour but lose about 60 calories from the dish.
Use chicken breast instead of thigh and drumstick. Less flavour, yes, but if you're counting calories the swap saves you 40 to 60 calories per serving.
Eat it with plain steamed rice and a pile of sayur manis or other low-calorie veg on the side. The dish pairs well with greens and you'll stay full without needing a second helping.

faq.q: How many calories in Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken)?
faq.a: Around 530 calories per serving of 2 to 3 bone-in chicken pieces with wine sauce, roughly 300g total. That's 30g protein, 6g carbs, and 35g fat. The sesame oil is the main calorie driver at about 180 calories on its own.

faq.q: What is Ayam Masak Arak exactly?
faq.a: It's a Foochow Chinese dish from Sibu, Sarawak where chicken is braised in ang chao (red glutinous rice wine) with sesame oil and ginger. It's traditionally a confinement dish eaten after childbirth but you'll also find it at Sarawakian kopitiam. The sauce has a slightly sweet, winey, deeply aromatic flavour from the wine dregs and sesame oil cooked together.

faq.q: Is Ayam Masak Arak a healthy dish?
faq.a: It depends what you mean by healthy. The protein is solid at 30g, the carbs are low at 6g, and ginger has its merits. But 35g fat and 530 calories for a side dish means it adds up fast if you're not careful with portions. The soup-style version at around 380 calories is a lighter option if you're watching your intake.

foods.name: Butter Prawns
foods.serving: 1 restaurant portion (6-8 medium-large prawns, shell-on, with egg floss)
foods.metaDescription: Butter Prawns clock around 580 calories per restaurant portion. The butter and egg floss add up fast. Full breakdown inside.
foods.summary: Shell-on prawns deep-fried then wok-tossed in a rich butter, curry leaf and egg-floss sauce, which is as good as it sounds and as calorie-heavy as you'd expect.
foods.answer: A restaurant portion of Butter Prawns (6-8 medium-large shell-on prawns with egg floss) comes in at around 580 calories, with 28g protein, 14g carbs and 44g fat. The prawns themselves are not the problem; it's the butter, the deep-frying oil and those crispy egg-yolk strands that stack the numbers fast. Note that this is a ballpark estimate because reliable lab data for this dish is thin, so treat it as a realistic guide rather than gospel.
realTalk: Butter Prawns is one of those dishes where the main ingredient is genuinely good for you and then the cooking method absolutely wrecks the macro profile. You get prawns, which are lean and high-protein, but they go into a deep fryer first, then get tossed in a wok with a generous amount of butter, evaporated milk, curry leaves, and egg-yolk floss fried in more butter. The egg floss alone contributes around 115 calories. The butter base adds another 130 calories. So out of 580 total calories, roughly 390 come from fat sources. If you've never had this dish, picture crispy golden prawns coated in a fragrant, slightly creamy sauce with delicate egg strands that melt on your tongue. It's genuinely one of the better things Malaysian Chinese cuisine has produced. Worth eating. Just not every day, lah.

The version you order matters a lot. A home-cooked pan-fried version with the same butter and egg floss but without deep-frying sits around 280 calories, basically half the restaurant number, because you skip the absorbed frying oil. The salted egg version pushes up to 640 calories because salted egg yolks replace or supplement the egg floss and those yolks are very fat-dense. Portion size is another big variable. A restaurant order is typically shared between two or three people alongside rice and vegetables, so your actual intake might be 180-200 calories per person if you split it properly. The calorie estimates here are best guesses since standardised data for this dish is genuinely hard to find, so treat the numbers as a solid ballpark rather than exact figures.
lighter: Share it properly. Split one restaurant portion between two people and you're looking at roughly 290 calories each, which is perfectly manageable.
Order the pan-fried version when you can, or ask at hawker stalls. Skipping the deep-fry step cuts about 80 calories straight away.
Eat it with plain steamed rice, not fried rice. The dish already has enough fat going on, you don't need more from the rice.
Go easy on the sauce at the bottom of the plate. A lot of the butter and oil pools there. You can leave it and lose maybe 50-80 calories.
Skip the salted egg upgrade. The regular egg floss version saves you around 60 calories per portion and honestly tastes just as good.

faq.q: How many calories in Butter Prawns?
faq.a: A standard restaurant portion of Butter Prawns, which is 6-8 medium-large shell-on prawns with egg floss sauce, contains around 580 calories. A home-cooked pan-fried version is closer to 280 calories, and the salted egg variant goes up to about 640 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is Butter Prawns and what makes it so rich?
faq.a: Butter Prawns is a Malaysian Chinese dish where shell-on prawns are deep-fried then wok-tossed in a sauce of butter, evaporated milk and curry leaves, finished with crispy egg-yolk floss. The combination of deep-frying oil absorbed by the prawns plus the butter sauce base is what drives the calorie count so high. The egg floss alone adds around 115 calories to the dish.

faq.q: Is Butter Prawns a good source of protein or should I avoid it when dieting?
faq.a: The prawns themselves are solid protein at around 28g per portion, which is decent. The problem is the fat coming in at 44g, mostly from butter and frying oil. It's not a dish to avoid entirely, but it's better treated as an occasional order and shared between people rather than a solo serving. Pair it with plain rice and vegetables and you've got a reasonable meal overall.

foods.name: Chili Crab
foods.serving: 1 serving, about half a medium mud crab with sauce
foods.metaDescription: Chili crab is about 450 kcal per half crab with sauce. The sweet chili gravy and wok oil do the heavy lifting, not the crab meat itself.
foods.summary: Mud crab wok-tossed in a sweet, spicy tomato and chili sauce thickened with egg, served with mantou or rice and absolutely covered in sauce you will not stop mopping up.
foods.answer: Half a medium mud crab with sauce comes in at around 450 kcal, with 25g protein, 20g carbs, and 22g fat. The crab meat itself is actually lean at about 100 kcal for 120g edible meat. The calories come mostly from the wok oil (roughly 180 kcal per portion) and the sweet chili and ketchup sauce base (about 105 kcal for 60g). So yes, you are basically paying 280 kcal just for the sauce and oil that makes the whole thing taste incredible.
realTalk: Chili crab is a Singapore and Malaysian seafood classic, a whole mud crab cracked open and cooked in a glossy, slightly sweet, spicy tomato and chili gravy thickened with beaten egg. It looks dramatic, tastes amazing, and is genuinely a mess to eat. At 450 kcal for half a crab with sauce, it is not the worst thing in the world, but do not let the word "crab" fool you into thinking this is some low-calorie health food. The crab meat is lean, sure. But the sauce is built on ketchup, sweet chili sauce, and a generous pour of wok oil, and that is where most of the damage happens. Worth flagging: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid nutritional data for chili crab is basically non-existent. Different hawkers use different amounts of oil and sauce, so treat 450 kcal as a reasonable middle-ground, not gospel.

What actually moves the number is the oil and the sauce. Some stalls are heavy-handed with the wok oil, which alone can push your portion past 200 kcal before you even count the crab. The sweet chili and ketchup base adds another 100-plus kcal for 60g of sauce, and people mop that up. The bread is where it gets serious though: two steamed mantou add about 160 kcal, taking you to 610 kcal total. Two fried mantou, which soak up oil, push it to 650 kcal. Swap to a bowl of white rice and you are at 680 kcal. If you want to keep it lower, eat the crab plain with no bread and go easy on scooping up the gravy. The crab meat itself is genuinely high protein and not the problem here.
lighter: Skip the mantou entirely. Two fried mantou alone add 200 kcal on top of your 450 kcal crab, which is a big chunk for bread you are mostly using to mop sauce.
Go easy on the sauce. I know it is the best part, but 60g of that sweet chili gravy is already 105 kcal. Leave some in the pot instead of chasing every last drop.
Order steamed mantou over fried if you need the bread. Steamed is roughly 80 kcal per bun versus fried, which absorbs oil and costs more.
Share the crab. A whole mud crab with two people plus shared rice keeps your individual total way more manageable than going solo.
Pair it with a plain steamed vegetable dish, something like kailan or kangkung, instead of rice or noodles to keep the overall meal calories reasonable while still feeling full.

faq.q: How many calories in Chili Crab?
faq.a: About 450 kcal for half a medium mud crab with sauce, roughly 250g. That breaks down to 25g protein, 20g carbs, and 22g fat. Add steamed mantou and you are at 610 kcal, fried mantou brings it to 650 kcal, and a bowl of rice takes it to 680 kcal.

faq.q: What exactly is chili crab?
faq.a: It is a whole mud crab cooked in a wok with a thick, sweet and spicy sauce made from chili, ketchup, tomato, and egg. The sauce is glossy, slightly tangy, a bit sweet, and very orange. You eat it with your hands, crack the shell yourself, and use bread or rice to mop up the sauce. It is messy and very worth it.

faq.q: Is chili crab actually healthy?
faq.a: The crab meat itself is lean and high in protein, 120g of edible meat is only about 100 kcal. The problem is the sauce and wok oil, which together add close to 340 kcal per serving. So it is decent protein for the calories, but not a low-calorie meal, especially once you add bread or rice on the side.

foods.name: Ikan Pari Bakar (Grilled Stingray)
foods.serving: 1 serving, hawker stall (stingray wing in banana leaf with sambal)
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Pari Bakar clocks around 430 calories per hawker serving. The stingray is lean, it's the sambal and grilling oil that add up. Full breakdown here.
foods.summary: Stingray wing grilled in banana leaf and smothered in sambal belacan, a hawker classic that is honestly one of the better high-protein options at the stall if you watch the oil.
foods.answer: One hawker serving of Ikan Pari Bakar (a full stingray wing in banana leaf with sambal belacan, about 320g) comes to around 430 calories, with 44g protein, 10g carbs, and 22g fat. The fish itself is surprisingly lean at only 195 calories for the whole wing portion. The sambal and the oil absorbed during grilling are doing most of the calorie work.
realTalk: Ikan pari bakar is stingray wing grilled directly on a charcoal or gas flame, wrapped in banana leaf and heaped with sambal belacan made from fermented shrimp paste (belacan), chilli, shallots, and lime. It is a hawker staple all over the peninsula, most famously in Melaka and the seafood town stalls along the coasts. The fish itself is lean and meaty, which is why the protein number (44g) is genuinely impressive for a single dish. The catch is that the calories are sitting at 430 because of 160 calories worth of cooking oil absorbed during grilling and another 75 from the sambal. Be honest: this is a solid protein source dressed up in a fairly oily sauce. These numbers are a ballpark estimate because detailed nutrition data for stingray specifically is thin, so treat the figures as a reasonable middle ground rather than lab-certified truth.

What actually changes the maths is how generous the stall is with oil and sambal. A home-style version with minimal basting and a thinner sambal layer can bring things down to around 320 calories for the same wing. On the other end, some pasar malam stalls add a margarine or extra oil baste on top, which pushes it past 550 calories. The wing size matters too: a bigger wing at 270g of flesh instead of 230g adds roughly 40 to 50 more calories from the fish alone. If you are eating this with rice, that is another 250 to 350 calories depending on how much you scoop, so plan accordingly. The good news is you can ask the stall to go light on the sambal and skip any butter baste, and you are looking at something closer to 350 calories with 44g protein, which is a pretty solid deal lah.
lighter: Ask the stall to go easy on the oil baste. Some places douse the whole thing before serving. Just ask, most will oblige.
Skip or halve the sambal topping. The sambal belacan adds about 75 calories and a good chunk of the sodium. A smaller scoop still gives you all the flavour.
Eat it with plain steamed rice or extra kangkung rather than nasi lemak or fried rice. The fish itself is doing the heavy lifting protein-wise.
Avoid the pasar malam versions with margarine or butter baste on top. That one extra step adds well over 100 calories to an already decent dish.
Share one wing between two people and order an extra plate of blanched vegetables. The portion is filling enough to split, and you get more variety on the table for the same calories.

faq.q: How many calories in Ikan Pari Bakar (Grilled Stingray)?
faq.a: A standard hawker serving of Ikan Pari Bakar, one stingray wing in banana leaf with sambal belacan (around 320g), comes to about 430 calories. That is 44g protein, 10g carbs, and 22g fat. These are estimates as detailed nutrition data for stingray is limited, but they represent a reasonable middle-ground figure for a typical hawker portion.

faq.q: What exactly is Ikan Pari Bakar?
faq.a: Ikan pari is stingray and bakar means grilled. The wing is laid on a banana leaf, smothered in sambal belacan (a paste of fermented shrimp paste (belacan), chilli, shallots, and lime), then grilled over charcoal or gas until the banana leaf chars at the edges and the fish is cooked through. It is a hawker classic across Malaysia, particularly popular at seafood stalls in Melaka, Klang, and coastal towns. The flesh is firm, slightly sweet, and soaks up the spicy sambal really well.

faq.q: Is Ikan Pari Bakar a healthy option for someone trying to lose weight?
faq.a: Honestly, it is one of the better things you can order at a hawker stall if protein is your goal. 44g protein for 430 calories is a good ratio. The fish itself is lean, and the calories mainly come from the sambal and grilling oil, both of which you can ask to be reduced. Compared to a plate of char kuey teow or curry laksa at similar or higher calories but much less protein, this comes out ahead. Just watch the rice portion you pair it with.

foods.name: Nasi Kukus
foods.serving: 1 plate (steamed rice + 1 piece ayam goreng berempah + sambal + sides)
foods.metaDescription: Nasi Kukus is about 700 calories per plate, steamed rice with crispy spiced fried chicken. Here is what drives the count and how to order smarter.
foods.summary: Steamed rice served with ayam goreng berempah and sambal, a classic at mamak stalls and East Coast hawker spots where the crispy spiced fried chicken is the whole point.
foods.answer: A standard plate of Nasi Kukus comes in at around 700 calories: 220g of steamed rice (285 kcal), one piece of ayam goreng berempah at 150g (300 kcal), sambal at about 55 kcal, and the usual sides of ikan bilis, cucumber and tauge adding another 50 kcal. The fried chicken alone is doing nearly half the work here, so that is where the number lives.
realTalk: Nasi Kukus is basically steamed rice served with a piece of heavily spiced, deep-fried chicken (ayam goreng berempah), sambal, and a small pile of sides. It sounds simple but that one piece of fried chicken is pulling 300 calories on its own because it is coated in rempah paste and deep-fried. The rice and sambal are pretty tame by comparison. At 700 calories for a full plate with decent protein at 36g, it is not a disaster of a meal, honestly. If you were 128kg and eating two of these plates, yes, that is a problem. But one plate fits into a sensible day without much drama. Fair warning though: calorie data for nasi kukus is thin and the numbers here are a ballpark estimate based on component weights. Different stalls use different amounts of oil and rempah, so treat 700 kcal as a reasonable middle ground, not a lab-certified figure.

The single biggest lever is the gravy. If you go kuah banjir style, where the uncle floods your rice with curry gravy, you are looking at around 1,100 calories instead of 700. That extra ladle of curry adds close to 400 kcal in one move. Ordering a second piece of ayam goreng berempah bumps you straight to 980 calories. If you want to eat lighter, skip the ikan bilis (saves you roughly 70 calories and a bit of fat from the frying), ask for less sambal, and stick to one piece of chicken. The steamed rice portion is actually quite reasonable at 220g for 285 kcal, so the rice is not your enemy here. It is the oil in the chicken and any add-on gravy that pushes the number up fast.
lighter: Stick to one piece of ayam goreng berempah and skip any extra chicken. Going from one to two pieces adds 280 calories.
Say no to kuah banjir. That curry gravy pour-over adds close to 400 calories in one move and you barely notice it taste-wise.
Skip the ikan bilis goreng if you are watching calories. It is fried anchovies, which adds fat you do not really need when the chicken already has plenty.
Load up on the cucumber and tauge sides instead. They add almost no calories and actually help you feel fuller.
If the stall lets you choose your chicken cut, go for whatever you prefer. Drumstick, thigh, the fat difference between cuts is small either way.

faq.q: How many calories in Nasi Kukus?
faq.a: A standard plate of Nasi Kukus is around 700 calories: 285 kcal from the steamed rice, 300 kcal from one piece of ayam goreng berempah, 55 kcal from the sambal, and about 50 kcal from the ikan bilis and vegetable sides.

faq.q: What exactly is Nasi Kukus?
faq.a: Nasi Kukus means steamed rice, but the dish is really about the ayam goreng berempah, which is a deep-fried chicken piece coated in a blend of spices like turmeric, lemongrass, and galangal. It is popular at mamak stalls and East Coast hawker places in Malaysia, and you will also find it commonly in Sabah. The rice is plain steamed, but the chicken is anything but.

faq.q: Is Nasi Kukus healthy for someone trying to lose weight?
faq.a: One plate at 700 calories with 36g of protein is actually a decent meal for weight loss, as long as you stop at one plate. The fried chicken is high in fat from the oil, so it is not the leanest protein source, but the portion is not huge. The danger is adding curry gravy (jumps to 1,100 kcal) or ordering two pieces of chicken (980 kcal). Keep it to one piece, no gravy flood, and it fits into a calorie deficit without feeling like punishment.

foods.name: Daun Ubi Tumbuk
foods.metaDescription: Daun ubi tumbuk is around 270 calories per warung serving. The cassava leaves are basically free, but the santan does the heavy lifting calorie-wise.
foods.summary: Pounded young cassava leaves slow-cooked with thick coconut milk, lemongrass, and ikan bilis, a staple side dish in Sarawak and Sabah that tastes humble but hits harder than it looks.
foods.answer: A standard hawker or warung serving of daun ubi tumbuk (about 170g) comes in at roughly 270 calories, with 9g protein, 9g carbs, and 20g fat. The leaves themselves are almost nothing calorie-wise. It is the santan that carries the bulk of the calories, contributing around 135 calories out of the 270 on its own.
realTalk: Daun ubi tumbuk is basically pounded cassava leaves cooked down in coconut milk with aromatics and usually ikan bilis or anchovies. If you have never had it, think of it as Sarawak and Sabah's answer to a braised greens side dish, except the gravy is rich, slightly fatty, and really good with rice. At 270 calories for a side dish, it is not exactly a free food, but it is not crazy either. The cassava leaves themselves only contribute about 30 calories. The santan is doing 135 calories of work all by itself. Be honest with yourself about how much gravy you are ladling over your rice. Fair warning on the numbers: this is a genuine ballpark estimate because there is basically no hard nutritional data published for this specific dish, and every warung makes it differently.

What actually moves the maths is simple: how much santan and how much oil. The tanpa santan version (just oil, garlic, anchovies) drops to around 120 calories for the same-sized serving, saving you 150 calories. The light coconut milk version sits at 180 calories. Go full masak santan pekat with generous coconut milk and maybe some udang or offal thrown in and you are looking at 400 calories from a side dish alone. The ikan bilis adds about 45 calories but also gives you a protein hit for the size. If you are eating this at a nasi campur counter, watch the portion size because the serving spoon will give you whatever it gives you, and the gravy tends to be generous.
lighter: Ask for tanpa santan or kurang santan if you are at a place that makes it fresh, you can drop from 270 to 120-180 calories easily.
Eat it with plain white rice rather than nasi lemak or nasi minyak. The dish is already fatty, no need to stack coconut rice on top.
Treat it as a condiment, not a main. Two big spoonfuls of the dish alongside a leaner protein like ikan stim or ayam bakar keeps total calories in check.
Skip extra gravy. The leaves are fine, it is the pooled santan at the bottom of the tray that inflates the number. Take the solids.
Pair it with a clear soup rather than another santan-based lauk. Your body does not know which meal the fat came from, so keep the rest of the plate lighter.

faq.a: A typical hawker or warung serving of daun ubi tumbuk (170g) is around 270 calories, with 9g protein, 9g carbs, and 20g fat. The coconut milk accounts for the majority of those calories.

faq.q: What exactly is daun ubi tumbuk?
faq.a: It is young cassava leaves that get pounded, then cooked slowly in coconut milk with lemongrass, shallots, turmeric, chili, and usually ikan bilis or salted fish. It is a classic side dish in Sarawak and Sabah, commonly eaten with rice at warung and nasi campur stalls.

faq.q: Is daun ubi tumbuk a healthy vegetable dish?
faq.a: The cassava leaves themselves are high in fibre and protein for a leafy green, and the ikan bilis contributes some protein too. The catch is the thick santan, which pushes the fat to 20g and the total to 270 calories for a side dish. It is fine in context, just do not assume it is calorie-free because it is listed under vegetables.

foods.name: Wild Boar (Babi Hutan)
foods.serving: 1 serving wild boar dish (meat + gravy, no rice)
foods.metaDescription: Wild boar curry (babi hutan) comes in at around 460 calories per serving, with 54g protein. Non-halal. Here is what drives those numbers.
foods.summary: Wild boar, or babi hutan, is a non-halal game meat popular in Sabah and Sarawak, cooked as curry, stir-fry with bamboo shoot, or smoked, and it is leaner and gamier than the farmed pork you know.
foods.answer: A standard serving of wild boar dish (about 290g of meat and gravy, no rice) comes to roughly 460 calories, with 54g protein, 23g fat, and only 5g carbs. That is for the curry version, which is the base estimate here. Smoked wild boar (sinalau bakas) drops to around 310 calories, while adding santan to the curry pushes it up to 540 calories.
realTalk: Babi hutan is a Borneo thing, mainly Sabah and Sarawak, and it is worth knowing about if you have never had it. This is wild game, not farmed pork, so the meat itself is leaner and a lot gamier in flavour. At 460 calories for a curry serving, the number is solid for what you get: 54g of protein is genuinely impressive, and the carbs are almost nothing since it is just meat and spices. The fat at 23g is moderate, not alarming. Honestly this is a pretty decent dish for a dieter if you are not Muslim and you happen to be eating in Sabah or Sarawak. Fair warning though: hard nutrition data for wild boar cooked the Malaysian way is basically nonexistent, so these numbers are a ballpark estimate based on the closest data available. Do not treat them as gospel.

What really shifts the maths here is the cooking method and the gravy. Sinalau bakas, the smoked version where the meat is just salted and dried over fire, skips most of the oil entirely and comes in at about 310 calories for a similar portion. The moment you add a curry paste and cooking oil, you are looking at 108 extra calories just from the oil absorbed into the dish. Throw in coconut milk and the whole thing jumps to 540 calories. So if you are watching numbers, ask for the stir-fry with bamboo shoot (tumis babi hutan) at around 400 calories, go easy on the gravy, and skip the santan version. Pair it with rice and a full plate sits around 720 calories, which is fine for a meal as long as you account for it.
lighter: Order sinalau bakas where available. The smoked preparation skips the curry paste and most of the oil, cutting about 150 calories from the same amount of meat.
Skip the santan. Coconut milk adds roughly 80 calories to an already decent curry, and the dish honestly tastes great without it.
Go easy on the gravy. Most of the oil calories pool in the sauce, so scoop the meat and leave some of the liquid behind.
Ask for the bamboo shoot stir-fry version (tumis babi hutan) instead of curry. Less gravy, less oil, about 60 fewer calories.

Watch your rice portion. The meat itself is high protein and low carb, so do not cancel it out with a mountain of rice. Stick to 150g cooked rice instead of 200g and you save around 65 calories from the full plate total.

faq.q: How many calories in Wild Boar (Babi Hutan)?
faq.a: A standard serving of wild boar curry (about 290g of meat and gravy, no rice) is around 460 calories. Smoked wild boar (sinalau bakas) is closer to 310 calories, while wild boar curry with coconut milk reaches about 540 calories. Add 200g of white rice and a full plate is around 720 calories.

faq.q: What is babi hutan and is it halal?
faq.a: Babi hutan literally means wild forest pig. It is game meat hunted in the jungles of Sabah and Sarawak, and it is a staple in the indigenous communities of Borneo. It is non-halal, so this one is only for non-Muslim diners. The meat is leaner and gamier than farmed pork, and it is commonly cooked as a curry, stir-fried with bamboo shoot, or smoked over fire as sinalau bakas.

faq.q: Is wild boar good for weight loss?
faq.a: Actually not bad, if you choose the right preparation. At 54g of protein per serving and only 5g of carbs, the meat itself is lean and filling. The calories mainly come from cooking oil and gravy. Stick to the smoked or stir-fried versions, go easy on the sauce, and it is a genuinely high-protein meal that fits into a calorie deficit without too much fuss.

foods.name: Sago Gula Melaka
foods.metaDescription: Sago Gula Melaka has around 370 calories per hawker bowl. The gula melaka syrup and thick santan are where most of it comes from, not the sago.
foods.summary: Chilled sago pearls drowned in fragrant palm sugar syrup and poured over with thick coconut milk, served cold and way too easy to finish in two minutes.
foods.answer: A hawker bowl of Sago Gula Melaka comes in at around 370 calories for a 250g serving. The sago pearls themselves are pretty light at 155 calories for 120g, but the gula melaka syrup adds another 115 calories and the thick santan poured on top contributes around 100 calories. So basically, you are paying most of your calorie tab to the syrup and coconut milk, not the sago. Total carbs sit at 62g, fat at 13g, and protein at just 2g.
realTalk: Sago Gula Melaka is one of those desserts that looks innocent because it is mostly translucent pearls in a bowl, but the two liquids poured over it are doing the heavy lifting calorie-wise. Gula melaka is real palm sugar, fragrant and genuinely delicious, and santan is full-fat coconut milk. Together they account for 215 out of the 370 calories. To be straight with you, the 370 figure here is a ballpark estimate because there is very little hard published data specifically for this dish, and portion sizes vary a lot between hawkers. A light version with minimal santan might be closer to 260 calories, a generous Nyonya-style pour can push to 460. If you have never had it before, think of it as the Malaysian answer to a pudding dessert, chilled, slightly sweet, with that distinct smoky-caramel note from the palm sugar.

What actually moves the numbers is how heavy-handed the hawker is with the syrup and santan. A kopitiam that free-pours thick coconut milk adds way more than one where you get a thin drizzle. If you ask for less santan, you realistically knock off around 80 to 110 calories just from that one change, dropping the bowl to roughly 260 to 290 calories. The sago itself is almost entirely starch with negligible protein or fat, so there is no meaningful way to swap it out and still eat the same dish. Where you can control things: portion size matters more than anything else here. A small half-bowl at 125g would put you around 185 calories, which is perfectly reasonable as a dessert after a proper meal.
lighter: Ask for less santan or santan on the side. That single move saves you 80 to 110 calories without touching the gula melaka flavour.
If the place lets you choose your syrup amount, go half. The gula melaka is potent enough that half the syrup still gives you that full palm sugar hit.
Treat it as dessert, not a snack on top of dessert. A bowl after a protein-forward meal is fine. Two bowls because it is light-looking is not.
Order the small size if available. A 125g portion is roughly 185 calories, which is a very different number from the standard 250g hawker bowl.
Pair it with a zero-calorie drink like plain water or unsweetened iced Chinese tea instead of teh tarik, so the dessert stays the indulgence and does not stack onto an already heavy drink order.

faq.q: How many calories in Sago Gula Melaka?
faq.a: A standard hawker bowl of Sago Gula Melaka (250g) is around 370 calories. That breaks down to 155 calories from the sago pearls, 115 from the gula melaka syrup, and 100 from the thick coconut milk. Lighter versions with less santan can be as low as 260 calories, while a rich Nyonya-style serve can hit 460.

faq.q: What exactly is Sago Gula Melaka?
faq.a: It is a chilled Malaysian dessert made from cooked sago pearls, which are small translucent starch balls, served with gula melaka syrup made from palm sugar and poured over with thick coconut milk. You get it at kopitiams, pasar malams, and Nyonya restaurants. It is sweet, fragrant, and usually served cold.

faq.q: Is Sago Gula Melaka a healthy dessert?
faq.a: Honestly, it is not a diet food, but it is not the worst dessert either. At 370 calories per bowl it is lighter than most cakes or fried desserts, but it is almost entirely carbs and fat with barely any protein. If you ask for less coconut milk you can bring it down to around 260 calories, which is reasonable as an occasional treat.

foods.name: Tenom Coffee
foods.serving: 1 cup (standard hawker/kopitiam serve, kopi putih with condensed milk)
foods.metaDescription: Tenom Coffee (kopi putih) runs about 130 calories a cup, mostly from condensed milk. Kopi O kosong? Nearly zero. Here is what you are actually drinking.
foods.summary: Tenom Coffee is a wok-roasted Sabah robusta from the Tenom valley, famous for its deep, smoky kick, and the calories swing wildly depending on how much condensed milk goes in.
foods.answer: A standard cup of Tenom kopi putih (white coffee with condensed milk) comes in at around 130 calories. That is the full hawker-style serve with roughly 28g of sweetened condensed milk and a small hit of added sugar on top. Go kopi O kosong (black, no sugar, no milk) and you are looking at about 5 calories. The coffee itself does almost nothing to your calorie count. It is entirely what you put IN it that matters.
realTalk: Tenom Coffee is a big deal in Sabah. The beans come from the Tenom valley, wok-roasted by Yit Foh, and the result is a thick, aromatic robusta with a smoky depth that tastes nothing like your generic instant stuff. If you have never had it, think strong kopitiam kopi but with more character. The calorie numbers here are honest estimates, bah, because there is no hard nutrition data published for this specific coffee, so treat them as ballpark figures based on the ingredients. For the standard kopi putih with condensed milk, 130 calories sounds modest but it adds up fast if you drink two or three a day.

What actually drives the calories is straightforward: condensed milk, full stop. That 28g of condensed milk alone is 90 calories. The brewed coffee itself is basically 5 calories. So if you switch from kopi putih to kopi C (evaporated milk plus sugar), you drop from 130 to about 90 calories per cup. Go kopi O with sugar and you are at 65 calories. Go kopi O kosong and you are at 5. Three cups of kopi putih a day is 390 calories before you have eaten a single thing. Three cups of kopi O kosong is 15 calories. That is the whole game right there.
lighter: Order kopi O kosong if you can handle bitter coffee. Five calories per cup, and after a week you stop noticing the sweetness is gone.
Switch to kopi C (evaporated milk, no sugar) if you need something a bit smoother. About 40 calories versus 130 for the full condensed milk version.
If you must have kopi putih, ask them to go light on the susu (milk). A smaller pour of condensed milk can shave 30 to 40 calories off each cup easily.
Count your cups. Two kopi putih a day is 260 calories. That is a full snack just from drinks. Three cups and you are drinking a small meal.
Drink it hot. Kopi peng (iced) gets a slightly heavier pour of condensed milk to handle the ice dilution, pushing it to about 135 calories.

faq.q: How many calories in Tenom Coffee?
faq.a: A standard cup of Tenom kopi putih with condensed milk is around 130 calories. Kopi O kosong (black, no sugar) is about 5 calories. Kopi C with sugar sits at roughly 90 calories. The coffee itself is near zero; it is the condensed milk and sugar doing the work.

faq.q: What exactly is Tenom Coffee?
faq.a: Tenom Coffee is a robusta coffee grown and wok-roasted in the Tenom district of Sabah, Malaysia. The main brand is Yit Foh. It has a stronger, smokier flavour than most Peninsula Malaysian kopitiams serve, and it is a genuine point of pride in Sabah. You will find it served as kopi O (black), kopi C (evaporated milk), or kopi putih (white, with condensed milk).

faq.q: Is Tenom Coffee a healthy drink?
faq.a: The coffee part is fine, bro. Black coffee has basically no calories and the caffeine is a bonus. The problem is the condensed milk and sugar. A kopi putih a day is manageable. Three cups of kopi putih a day is nearly 400 calories from drinks alone, which will quietly wreck your deficit if you are not paying attention. Go black or go evaporated milk and you are in good shape.

foods.name: Air Barli
foods.metaDescription: Air barli from a kopitiam glass is about 100 calories, almost all from sugar. Here's what you're actually drinking and how sweet matters.
foods.summary: Air barli is a Malaysian barley drink made by boiling pearl barley with rock sugar until the water turns slightly milky and sweet, often served cold at kopitiams and hawker stalls.
foods.answer: A standard 300ml kopitiam glass of air barli comes in at about 100 calories. Most of that is from the dissolved rock sugar, around 48 calories from roughly 2.5 teaspoons of sweetener. The pearl barley itself contributes about 52 calories of starch that leaches into the water during boiling. So yeah, this is basically flavoured sugar water with a faint grain taste. Not terrible in the grand scheme of Malaysian drinks, but the calories are almost entirely carbs (24g), zero fat, barely any protein.
realTalk: Air barli is one of those drinks you grab at the kopitiam when you want something that feels healthy, and honestly it's not wrong to think that way. Compared to teh tarik or Milo ais, 100 calories for a full glass is pretty decent. The drink is just boiled pearl barley water sweetened with rock sugar, sometimes with a squeeze of lemon if you order barli limau. The barley grain barely shows up calorie-wise since most of it stays solid and you're drinking the water, not eating the grain. To be upfront: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid nutrition data for kopitiam air barli is pretty thin, and sweetness levels vary from stall to stall.

What actually moves the calorie count here is simple: sugar. A lightly sweetened glass sits around 100 calories, but a generous auntie who pre-sweetens a whole pot heavily can push you to 130 calories without you knowing. Barli kosong with no sugar at all drops to around 30 calories, basically just hot grain water. Barli limau adds maybe 10 calories from the lemon and sometimes a touch more sugar to balance the sourness, landing around 110 calories. If you order frequently, asking for kosong or kurang manis is an easy way to shave 50 to 70 calories per glass across a week without feeling like you're giving up anything.
lighter: Order barli kosong or kurang manis. No sugar or less sugar drops it from 100 calories down to 30 to 60, and the drink still tastes like barley water.
Barli limau kosong is a solid option. The lemon gives it enough flavour that you don't miss the sweetness as much.
Skip the refill at the self-serve stalls. That second glass is another 100 calories you probably didn't plan for.
Drink it hot. Hot drinks tend to get sipped slower, so you drink less overall.
If you're making it at home, use stevia or skip the sweetener entirely. The barley starch gives a faint natural sweetness on its own.

faq.q: What is air barli exactly?
faq.a: Air barli is pearl barley boiled in water with rock sugar until the liquid turns slightly cloudy and sweet. You drink the liquid, not the grain. It's a common kopitiam and hawker stall drink served cold or hot, sometimes with lemon (barli limau). It's been around Malaysian coffee shops forever.

faq.q: Is air barli a healthy drink?
faq.a: Compared to teh tarik or Milo ais, 100 calories for a full glass is actually on the lower end for kopitiam drinks. There's no fat and no real protein either, so it's essentially sweetened water. It's fine as an occasional drink. If you want it to work for a diet, ask for kosong or kurang manis.

foods.name: Coffee Bun (Rotiboy)
foods.metaDescription: One Rotiboy coffee bun is about 340 calories for a single 85g bun. Small thing, big number. Here is what is going on inside.
foods.summary: A soft, pillowy bun with a butter core and a crisp coffee-cream shell baked on top, the Rotiboy-style coffee bun is one of those snacks that tastes way too good to be innocent calorie-wise.
foods.answer: One coffee bun (Rotiboy-style) comes in at around 340 calories for an 85g bun. That is 6g protein, 42g carbs, and 16g fat. It is a snack-sized thing that eats like a treat, and the numbers reflect exactly that.
realTalk: The coffee bun is basically a soft enriched bread roll with a cold butter core and a crunchy coffee-flavoured cream topping that bakes into a shell. Think of it as a hybrid between a dinner roll and a pastry. If you have never had one, the appeal is real: you bite through the slightly crisp top into soft bread, hit that pool of melting butter in the middle, and it just works. The 340 calories in one bun come from three layers of calorie-dense ingredients: the enriched dough made with egg, milk and sugar (190 cal), the butter filling (72 cal from just 10g of butter), and the coffee cream topping (78 cal from another hit of butter plus sugar). To be straight with you, hard calorie data on these buns is thin, so treat this 340 figure as a solid ballpark estimate, not a lab-verified number. The actual count can shift depending on how generous the baker is with the butter core.

Where the maths gets interesting is in how many you eat. One bun at 340 cal is a decent snack. Two buns is 680 cal, which is already a full meal worth of calories in something you ate standing at a kiosk in 4 minutes. The butter filling varies a lot too: some places are stingy (maybe 5-7g butter, closer to 35-50 cal) while others are extremely generous (15g butter, pushing 107 cal). That single variable alone can swing the bun by 50 to 70 calories. If you are in a deficit and want one, eat it fresh and hot so one bun is genuinely satisfying, and skip the teh tarik or kopi that usually comes alongside it.
lighter: Eat just one, fresh out of the oven. The experience is much more satisfying when it is hot, so you are less likely to reach for a second.
Skip the coffee or teh tarik pairing. A plain water or unsweetened ice tea alongside keeps the snack from becoming a 500-plus calorie break without you realising.
If you are baking at home, you can halve the butter filling from 10g down to 5g and save around 35 calories per bun without ruining it.
Treat it as a snack that replaces a meal component, not one that adds on top. If you are having a coffee bun at 3pm, eat a lighter dinner.
Buy from smaller bakeries or pasar malam stalls where the buns are genuinely small. Kiosk chain versions can be noticeably bigger than 85g, which pushes the calories higher.

components.name: Soft enriched bun dough (bread flour, egg, milk, sugar)
Coffee cream topping (butter, sugar, egg, flour, instant coffee)

faq.q: How many calories in Coffee Bun (Rotiboy)?
faq.a: One Rotiboy-style coffee bun is approximately 340 calories for an 85g bun, with 6g protein, 42g carbs, and 16g fat. This is a ballpark estimate as precise data for these buns is limited.

faq.q: What exactly is a coffee bun?
faq.a: It is a soft, enriched bread bun with a cold butter core and a crisp coffee-flavoured cream shell baked on top. The Rotiboy brand from Malaysia popularised it. You eat it warm and the butter inside melts as you bite through. It is a snack, not a meal, but the calories are closer to a meal than you would expect.

faq.q: Is a coffee bun a healthy snack?
faq.a: Not really, lah. At 340 calories with 16g fat mostly from butter, it is a treat snack. The protein is only 6g so it is not going to keep you full for long either. One a week is fine if you are in a deficit. The problem is that one rarely stays one.

foods.name: Teh O Limau Ais
foods.metaDescription: Teh O Limau Ais has about 70 calories per glass, almost all from sugar. Order kurang manis and you drop it to 40 cal. Here is the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Iced black tea with calamansi lime and sugar, no milk, making it one of the lighter drink options at any mamak or kopitiam.
foods.answer: A standard glass of Teh O Limau Ais is around 70 calories, almost entirely from the sugar the hawker adds. The black tea itself contributes basically nothing (about 2 calories), and the lime juice adds maybe 8. So the whole drink is basically just sweetened lime tea over ice. Order kurang manis and you are down to about 40 calories. These are ballpark estimates as hard data for this specific drink is thin, but the numbers are in the right range.
realTalk: Teh O Limau Ais is iced black tea with calamansi lime and sugar, no condensed milk involved. That is exactly why it is lighter than teh tarik, which can clock 130 to 180 calories from condensed milk alone. At 70 calories for a standard glass, it is honestly one of the better drink choices at a mamak. The problem is the word 'standard' does different things in different shops. Some hawkers have a heavy hand with the sugar, and a manis-heavy pour can push you to 100 calories easily. These numbers are estimates, bro, there is no lab testing happening here, so treat them as a ballpark.

What actually moves the calorie count is purely the sugar. The tea and lime are basically free calories. About three and a half teaspoons of sugar gets you to 70 calories. Four teaspoons lands at 100. One and a half teaspoons (kurang manis) puts you at about 40. If you are tracking, just say kurang manis every single time and you shave off 30 calories per glass. Over a day of two or three drinks, that adds up. Nothing else changes here, no oil, no protein, no noodle swap to worry about.
lighter: Order kurang manis every time, drops you from 70 to about 40 calories per glass.
If you want zero sugar, ask for teh o limau kosong. Pure tea and lime, basically zero calories.
Stick to one glass per meal rather than getting free refills at those all-you-can-drink spots.
Compare to teh tarik at 130 to 180 calories or milo ais at 250 plus, and teh o limau ais is already the smart pick lah.
Squeeze extra lime yourself if the stall has fresh limes on the table. More lime flavour means you notice the sweetness less even with less sugar.

faq.q: How many calories in Teh O Limau Ais?
faq.a: About 70 calories for a standard hawker glass at normal sweetness. Kurang manis brings it down to around 40 calories, and extra sweet can push it to 100. Almost all the calories come from sugar.

faq.q: What exactly is Teh O Limau Ais?
faq.a: It is iced black tea with calamansi lime juice and sugar, no milk. The 'O' means black (no milk) and 'limau' is lime. You will find it at pretty much every mamak, kopitiam, and hawker centre in Malaysia.

faq.q: Is Teh O Limau Ais a healthy drink choice?
faq.a: Compared to most Malaysian drinks it is one of the better options. No condensed milk, no Milo powder, no coconut milk. The only real calories come from sugar, so just say kurang manis and you have a 40-calorie drink that tastes good and keeps you hydrated. Not bad at all.

foods.name: Air Mata Kucing
foods.metaDescription: Air Mata Kucing has around 180 calories a glass at the hawker stall, mostly from rock sugar. Here is what you are actually drinking.
foods.summary: Air Mata Kucing is a classic Chinese herbal cooling drink made by boiling dried longan, monk fruit (luo han guo), and rock sugar together, then serving it iced.
foods.answer: A standard glass of Air Mata Kucing at your typical hawker stall or kopitiam clocks in at around 180 calories for a 300ml iced serving. Almost all of that comes from rock sugar: 40g dissolved into the drink alone contributes 154 calories. The dried longan bits you eat at the bottom add another 17. The monk fruit and winter melon that give it that herbal edge? Basically zero. So yeah, it tastes light and refreshing but calorie-wise it drinks more like a soft drink than plain water.
realTalk: Air Mata Kucing, which literally means "cat's eye tears" (named after the dried longan, not actual cats, relax), is a traditional Chinese cooling drink you find all over Malaysia. It is boiled from dried longan, monk fruit, sometimes winter melon strips, and a very generous hand with the rock sugar. The hawker version runs at about 180 calories per glass, and the honest truth is that is a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for this drink is basically nonexistent. Nobody has lab-tested the Petaling Street auntie's recipe. That said, the math is simple: rock sugar is still sugar, at roughly 4 calories per gram, and most stalls are not shy with it.

What actually swings the number is how heavy the sugar hand is. The home-cooked version using just 25g of rock sugar across a 1500ml pot works out to about 80 calories per glass, less than half the hawker version. The monk-fruit-only version drops to around 50 calories but good luck finding that at a stall. Bottled versions like Yeos or F&N sit around 120 calories because commercial production controls the sugar level. The ice dilutes the drink somewhat at the hawker stall but does not change the calorie count in any meaningful way since the sugar is already dissolved in the base liquid.
lighter: Ask for less sugar (kurang manis) if the stall lets you customise. Some will, some won't.
Make it at home. Use 20 to 25g of rock sugar per 1500ml of water instead of the 80 to 100g a typical hawker batch uses. Your glass drops from 180 to around 80 calories.
Go for the bottled version (Yeos, F&N) on the go. Around 120 calories and the sweetness is at least consistent.
Drink it slow and eat the longan bits at the bottom. That way you feel like you got something out of the glass instead of just chugging sugar water.

Compare it to your other drink options at the stall. At 180 calories it is actually worse than a can of Coke (139 calories for 330ml), which is a bit of a reality check for something that feels so light and herbal.

faq.q: How many calories in Air Mata Kucing?
faq.a: A standard hawker or kopitiam glass (about 300ml, iced) has around 180 calories. The vast majority comes from dissolved rock sugar, not the longan or monk fruit. Home-cooked versions can be as low as 80 calories if you go easy on the sugar.

faq.q: What exactly is Air Mata Kucing?
faq.a: It is a traditional Chinese herbal cooling drink made by simmering dried longan (the fruit), monk fruit (luo han guo), sometimes winter melon, and rock sugar in water, then serving it chilled or iced. The name means cat's eye tears in Malay, a reference to the small dried longan fruit. You find it at Chinese herbal drink stalls, kopitiam, and pasar malam all over Malaysia.

faq.q: Is Air Mata Kucing a healthy drink?
faq.a: It is not a bad choice compared to a teh tarik or sirap bandung, but it is not plain water either. The monk fruit has some antioxidant properties and the drink has zero fat, but 44g of carbs from sugar in one glass is real. If you are watching your calories, the home-cooked low-sugar version or a monk-fruit-only version is genuinely decent. The hawker stall version, though, is basically sweetened herbal water.

foods.name: Rojak Buah
foods.metaDescription: Rojak buah runs around 300 calories a plate. Sounds okay until you see how much of that comes from the sweet prawn paste and peanuts, not the fruit.
foods.summary: Rojak buah is a Malaysian fruit and vegetable salad with jambu, mango, pineapple, cucumber, and sengkuang, tossed in thick sweet hae ko sauce and finished with crushed peanuts.
foods.answer: A standard hawker plate of rojak buah is around 300 calories for roughly 250g. That number is a ballpark estimate since lab data for this dish is thin, but it's a reasonable figure for a typical portion with standard sauce and peanuts. The fruit itself is light; it's the hae ko sauce and the peanut topping doing most of the calorie work.
realTalk: Rojak buah looks like a fruit salad, so people assume it's basically free calories. It's not, but it's also not a disaster. The dish is fresh mixed fruit and vegetables, usually jambu air, mango, pineapple, cucumber, and sengkuang, tossed in a thick sauce made from hae ko (sweet fermented prawn paste), tamarind, and a fair amount of sugar. The whole plate comes in at around 300 calories for 250g, but here's the thing: the 160g of fruit only accounts for about 75 of those calories. The 55g of sauce contributes 130 calories, and the 22g of crushed peanuts on top adds another 125. So more than 80% of the calories come from the sauce and nuts, not the fruit. Fair heads up that these numbers are estimates because solid nutritional data for rojak buah is genuinely hard to find, so treat the figures as a useful ballpark rather than gospel.

What actually moves the needle here is how heavy-handed the uncle is with the sauce ladle and the peanut scoop. Ask for light sauce and less peanuts and you can realistically drop the plate down to around 200 calories. On the flip side, the Chinese-style version that comes with a stick of youtiao fried dough dunked in jumps to about 430 calories. The fruit portion itself barely changes things, so if you're watching numbers, your negotiation is entirely with the sauce and the peanuts. Order without youtiao, tell them to go light on the hae ko, and you've turned a 300-calorie snack into a 200-calorie one without feeling shortchanged.
lighter: Ask for less sauce. Seriously just say it. A light drizzle of hae ko instead of a full dunk can save you close to 60 to 70 calories on its own.
Skip the youtiao. The fried dough stick adds around 130 calories and is the single biggest upgrade to the calorie count.
Ask for less peanuts or skip them entirely. The 22g topping is adding 125 calories; even halving it makes a real difference.
Eat it as a proper snack, not a side dish stacked on top of a full meal. At 200 to 300 calories it fits fine as a standalone afternoon eat.
If you're making it at home, use a small measured amount of hae ko and go heavy on the sengkuang and cucumber since those are basically water with crunch and barely register calorically.

faq.a: A standard hawker plate of rojak buah is around 300 calories for a 250g serving. This is an estimate since hard data is thin for this dish, but it's a solid working figure. Light on sauce and peanuts brings it down to about 200 calories; add youtiao and you're looking at roughly 430 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is rojak buah?
faq.a: Rojak buah is a Malaysian mixed fruit and vegetable dish. You get a pile of fresh fruit (jambu air, mango, pineapple, cucumber, sengkuang) tossed in a thick, dark, sweet-savoury sauce made from hae ko (fermented prawn paste), tamarind, and sugar, then topped with crushed peanuts. It's tangy, sweet, a bit funky from the paste, and genuinely good. Common at pasar malam stalls and hawker centres across the country.

faq.q: Is rojak buah healthy?
faq.a: It's not bad, but it's not as light as it looks. The fruit base is fine but the hae ko sauce is high in sugar and the peanuts add a solid chunk of fat. At 300 calories it's a reasonable snack if you're keeping track. The main thing to watch is sodium from the prawn paste and the sugar load in the sauce, especially if you're having a big portion.

foods.name: Pasembur (Mamak Rojak)
foods.metaDescription: Pasembur (Mamak Rojak) is around 700 calories a plate. The prawn fritters and thick peanut sauce are the main culprits. Here is what you need to know.
foods.summary: Pasembur is a Penang mamak classic of shredded veg, fried tofu, prawn fritters, cuttlefish and boiled egg all drenched in a sweet, spicy peanut-and-sweet-potato sauce that absolutely does not mess around.
foods.answer: A standard hawker plate of Pasembur comes in at around 700 calories for roughly 430g of food. The vegetables and egg are basically free calories, but those prawn fritters alone clock in at 210 calories and the peanut sauce adds another 170. Load up the plate and you are easily looking at 950 calories before you sit down.
realTalk: Pasembur is one of those dishes that looks lighter than it is because half the plate is shredded cucumber and jicama. Do not be fooled lah. The real calorie drivers are the deep-fried prawn fritters (210 cal for 80g) and that thick, sweet peanut-and-sweet-potato sauce poured generously over everything (170 cal for 90g alone). Fried tofu strips bring another 120. The veg, cuttlefish and boiled egg together? Only about 160 calories total. So you have this beautiful pile of food that feels healthy but lands at 700 calories for a standard plate. Worth knowing: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid lab data on hawker pasembur is basically nonexistent. Every stall makes the sauce differently, fritters vary in size and oil absorption, so treat this as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually moves the numbers is how many fritters end up on your plate and how heavy-handed the uncle is with the sauce. Ask for less sauce and you are shaving off maybe 50 to 80 calories right there. Skip the prawn fritters entirely and go veg plus tofu only with light sauce and you drop the whole plate down to around 450 calories. That is a genuinely decent snack at that point. If you are ordering this as a full meal, know that at 700 calories it is on the heavier side for a snack, comparable to a full plate of char kuey teow. Better to treat it as a shared starter or a light solo meal rather than a side dish.
lighter: Ask for less sauce. The peanut sauce is the sneaky one, 170 calories in 90g. Half the pour, maybe 80 fewer calories.
Skip or reduce the prawn fritters. They are the single biggest calorie item at 210 calories. Go without and you have already cut nearly a third of the plate calories.
Load up on the shredded cucumber, jicama and bean sprouts. They are 50 calories for 120g. Ask the uncle to give you more veg.
Eat it as a standalone snack, not a side. At 700 calories it is already a meal on its own. Pairing it with rice or noodles is how you accidentally eat 1,200 calories at the hawker stall.
Share the plate. Split it two ways and it is a 350-calorie snack each, which is perfectly reasonable.

faq.q: How many calories in Pasembur (Mamak Rojak)?
faq.a: A standard hawker plate of Pasembur is around 700 calories for approximately 430g. A lighter version with less sauce and no prawn fritters drops to about 450 calories, while a loaded plate with extra fritters and double sauce can hit 950 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is Pasembur?
faq.a: Pasembur is a Penang hawker dish, sometimes called Mamak Rojak. It is a pile of shredded cucumber, jicama, bean sprouts, fried tofu, prawn fritters, cuttlefish and boiled egg, all topped with a thick sweet and spicy sauce made from peanuts and sweet potato. It is a mamak stall staple, especially in Penang.

faq.q: Is Pasembur a healthy choice?
faq.a: The vegetables and protein from the egg and cuttlefish are solid, but the deep-fried fritters and thick peanut sauce push the calorie count up fast. At 700 calories it is not a light snack. If you go easy on the fritters and sauce it becomes a much more reasonable option, but ordering the full loaded version regularly is going to make your deficit hard to maintain.

foods.name: Ais Krim (Local Ice Cream)
foods.metaDescription: Ais krim potong is about 80 calories per stick. Durian flavour hits 110 cal, red bean stays at 70. Here is the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Ais krim potong is the OG Malaysian ice cream on a stick, made with coconut milk and sugar, sold in flavours like red bean, corn, coconut, and durian.
foods.answer: One stick of ais krim potong is about 80 calories for a standard 65g bar. That is for your typical corn or coconut flavour. Red bean comes in lower at around 70 calories, while durian can push up to 110 calories per stick because durian puree is genuinely calorie-dense. The base is mostly sugar syrup and santan, so the calories are almost entirely carbs and fat, with barely any protein.
realTalk: Ais krim potong is the frozen treat you grew up eating from a styrofoam box at the school canteen or from a guy on a bicycle. It is a block of flavoured ice cream frozen on a stick, made with coconut milk, sugar syrup, and whatever filling goes in it, red bean, corn, pandan, or durian. At 80 calories a stick, it is actually one of the more reasonable desserts you can have. The calories come mainly from sugar (40 cal from sweeteners) and santan (17 cal). Durian is the only one you need to watch, at 110 cal per stick, because durian puree adds real density.

The math changes almost entirely by flavour choice. Red bean potong sits at 70 cal and the red bean filling actually adds a bit of fibre. Corn is 80 cal. Coconut is 85 cal, slightly richer santan base. Durian is 110 cal. So if you swap your durian stick for a red bean one you save 40 calories, which is real. Portion size also matters because some artisan or pasar malam versions are bigger than the standard 65g bar. A 90g homemade-style potong could easily be 120 cal. Stick to the individually wrapped commercial ones if you want predictable numbers.
lighter: Pick red bean flavour over durian. That swap alone cuts about 40 calories per stick.
Eat one stick, not two. Sounds obvious but pasar malam sellers sometimes push you to buy three for some deal.
Skip the big slab versions sold at dessert shops. Those are usually 150 cal or more per serving.
Buy the individually wrapped commercial bars like King's Potong where the calorie count is printed on the label.
Eat it as a standalone treat, not after a full meal. At 80 cal it is a fine dessert on its own.

faq.q: How many calories in Ais Krim (Local Ice Cream)?
faq.a: One standard stick of ais krim potong is about 80 calories (65g). Red bean flavour is around 70 cal, corn is 80 cal, coconut is 85 cal, and durian is the highest at around 110 cal per stick.

faq.q: What exactly is ais krim potong?
faq.a: It is a traditional Malaysian ice cream frozen in a rectangular block on a wooden stick. The base is coconut milk (santan) and sugar, with fillings like red bean, sweet corn, pandan, or durian. You will find it at school canteens, pasar malam, and convenience stores.

faq.q: Is ais krim potong healthy compared to other desserts?
faq.a: For a Malaysian dessert, it is actually on the lighter end. At 70 to 110 calories per stick it beats a bowl of cendol (around 330 cal) or ais kacang (around 350 cal) by a wide margin. The downside is it has almost no protein, so it is a treat, not a meal.

foods.name: Durian
foods.metaDescription: 4 seeds of durian is 175 calories. Eat a whole kampung durian and you're looking at 600 kcal. The numbers most people completely ignore.
foods.summary: Durian is the king of fruits in Malaysia, famously creamy, famously divisive, and famously more calorie-dense than almost any fruit you can name.
foods.answer: Four seeds of durian, roughly 120g of edible flesh, comes in at 175 calories. That sounds fine until you realise nobody stops at 4 seeds. A whole small kampung durian gives you around 400 to 500g of flesh, which lands at about 600 calories in one sitting. Musang King and Black Thorn push even higher per 100g, around 170 to 180 kcal per 100g, because the flesh is richer and fattier. The calories come from two places: sugars (carbs are 32g per serving) and fat (6g per serving), which is unusually high for a fruit.
realTalk: Durian is not a light snack. It is a calorie-dense fruit that sits somewhere between a dessert and a meal. The richness you taste in a good Musang King or Black Thorn seed? That is fat, specifically oleic and linoleic acids, the same types you find in nuts and avocado. Not bad fat, but still fat, and fat has 9 kcal per gram. Add the natural sugars and you get a fruit that hits 147 kcal per 100g for standard D24 and up to 175 to 180 kcal per 100g for the premium grades. Most fruit sits at 50 to 80 kcal per 100g. Durian is basically in a different weight class.

The maths changes fast based on variety and portion. Four seeds of kampung durian is about 145 calories, manageable. Four seeds of Musang King is 210 calories. A full kampung durian at the pasar malam is 600 calories. That is nearly a full meal worth of calories from fruit alone, eaten while standing, usually followed by more food. If you are tracking, weigh the flesh or count seeds honestly. Going from 4 seeds to 8 seeds does not just feel like double the enjoyment, it is double the calories.
lighter: Stop at 4 seeds and actually mean it. Set the limit before you open the fruit, not halfway through.
Go kampung durian instead of Musang King or Black Thorn. You save 35 to 70 calories per sitting and the flavour difference is smaller than the price difference.
Eat it as your dessert after a lighter meal, not as a snack on top of a full dinner.
Avoid durian with sticky rice or any creamy preparations. Plain flesh is already rich enough without adding coconut milk on top.
Share a fruit with someone instead of buying one each. Bro, you do not need a whole durian to yourself.
